title: Quarto
text:
Quarto is a Pandoc-based publishing system. A project is a directory with a _quarto.yml; quarto render walks it, runs each input through Pandoc, and writes a site to an output directory.
These pages cover the parts of a website project: configuration, the Pandoc dialect and format options, SCSS theming, navigation, listings, Lua filters, diagrams, directory-level metadata, and publishing.
Current version: Quarto 1.9

title: Directory Metadata
text:
A _metadata.yml in any directory supplies frontmatter to every document in that directory and below. It is merged into each document’s own frontmatter at render time.
The file uses the same keys a document’s frontmatter would, without the --- fences.

title: Directory Metadata
text:
Precedence
Narrowest wins. For any single key:

document frontmatter  >  nearest _metadata.yml  >  parent _metadata.yml  >  _quarto.yml

Scalars are replaced. Maps are merged key by key, so a document can override one nested option without restating the rest.
The leading underscore means the file is never treated as an input to render.

title: Directory Metadata
text:
What it is for
Anything that applies to a whole directory but does not belong in the individual files — a shared layout option, a class used to scope styles, a default format tweak for one section. It is also the place for options when the documents themselves are generated or mirrored from elsewhere, since edits to those files would not survive regeneration.

title: Listings
text:
A listing collects documents and renders them as a table, grid, or custom markup. It is declared in the frontmatter of the page that displays it.
In the page’s frontmatter, between its --- fences:
Then in the body, an empty div carrying the same id:
The id and the empty div with a matching #id are what place the output; without the div, Quarto appends the listing at the end of the page.

title: Listings
text:
Item fields
Each collected document contributes its frontmatter as fields. title, date, description, author, image, and categories (from the document’s categories key) are standard. Quarto also computes reading-time for listing items — it is a listing-level field, not something available inside the document itself.
A post is excluded by setting draft: true in its frontmatter.

title: Listings
Theming
text:
Quarto’s HTML format builds on Bootstrap. theme selects a base theme, custom SCSS, or a list combining both.
A bare name is one of the ~25 bundled Bootswatch themes. A path ending in .scss is a custom file. Quarto compiles the whole list into a single stylesheet in one Sass pass, so no runtime CSS loading is involved.

title: Theming
text:
Order is the cascade
Files are applied in list order. A rule in a later file overrides an equally specific rule in an earlier one, and a variable default in a later file is only used if no earlier file set it. Splitting a theme into several files — palette, base rules, per-component rules — therefore means ordering them from most general to most specific.
To confirm what order a build actually used, search the compiled bundle in _site/site_libs/bootstrap/ for a selector from each file and compare their positions.

title: Theming
Theming
text:
Icons
Quarto bundles Bootstrap Icons and loads the webfont on every page, so <i class="bi bi-cloud"></i> works with no setup. Config keys that accept an icon — navbar items, sidebar tools, callouts — take the name without the bi- prefix.
Any other icon set requires supplying the artwork, either as an inline SVG or as a file declared under project.resources.

title: Theming
section: Scoping styles to a subset of pages
text:
Scoping styles to a subset of pages
body-classes adds classes to <body>, so a rule can be written against a group of pages rather than all of them:

body-classes: blog-post

Set it in a _metadata.yml to apply it to a whole directory, then key the SCSS off .blog-post.

title: Project Config
text: _quarto.yml at the project root defines the project. Its presence is what makes a directory a Quarto project rather than a set of standalone documents.

title: Project Config
text:
Project block

project:
  type: website
  output-dir: _site

type selects the project kind — default, website, book, or manuscript. It determines which extra config blocks are recognised: a website project reads a website: block, a book reads book:.
output-dir is where the rendered site is written. It is cleaned and rewritten on render, so nothing hand-authored should live there.

title: Project Config
text:
Choosing inputs
By default a project renders every .qmd, .md, .ipynb, .rmd it finds, skipping directories that begin with . or _. An explicit render list overrides that:

project:
  render:
    - "*.qmd"
    - "*.md"
    - "!README.md"
    - "!docs/"

Entries are globs evaluated in order. A leading ! negates, removing previously matched files. Because the defaults already skip dot- and underscore-prefixed directories, files under .github/ or _extensions/ never need excluding.
A markdown file that is not meant to be a page — a README, contributor docs — will otherwise be rendered and published, since *.md matches it.

title: Project Config
text:
Resources
Quarto copies an asset to the output directory when it can see a reference to it: an image in markdown, a stylesheet in theme. Files referenced only from raw HTML or from JavaScript are invisible to that scan and must be declared:

project:
  resources:
    - assets/data.json
    - assets/js/late-loaded.js

Each entry is a path or glob relative to the project root, copied verbatim into output-dir.

title: Project Config
text:
Execution and freeze
For projects with executable code, execute: controls evaluation, and freeze caches results so documents are not re-executed on every render:

execute:
  freeze: auto

auto re-executes only when the source changes; true never re-executes; false always does. Frozen results are stored in _freeze/ and are meant to be committed, so a CI render does not need the computational environment.

title: Project Config
text:
Config precedence
Settings resolve from narrowest to widest: keys in a document’s own frontmatter beat a _metadata.yml in its directory, which beats _quarto.yml. See Directory Metadata.

title: Kitty Terminal
text:
Kitty is a free, open-source, and GPU-accelerated terminal emulator designed for Linux, macOS, and BSD systems.
The key features are:
- GPU Rendering: Offloads text rendering to the graphic card, making it fast and smooth compared to traditional CPU-based terminal emulators.
- Built-in Tiling & Tabs: Features an internal window manager that lets you split screens (horizontally/vertically) and use tabs without needing external tools like tmux.
- Scriptable & Extensible: Fully controlled via keyboard shortcuts and supports “Kittens” (small extensions) to do things like view images in the terminal or search for URLs.
- Modern Display Support: Supports TrueColor, ligatures, and specialized protocols for image rendering and keyboard input extensions.
What caught my interest was the GPU rendering, and built-in tiling and tabs.

title: Costs
text:
To capture the complete financial picture of moving a product from a factory floor to a customer’s hands, you must look at expenses across four distinct stages: Manufacturing, Landed Cost, Holding/Fulfillment, and Post-Sale.









Stage
Cost Category
Specific Expense Items




1. Manufacturing (Before Shipping)
Production Cost
Raw materials, factory labor, tooling/molds, and manufacturer markups.



Quality Control
Third-party inspection fees, laboratory testing, and sample creation.


2. Landed Cost (During Transit)
Product Price
The actual wholesale or FOB (Free on Board) price paid to the supplier.



Freight & Shipping
Ocean/air freight, fuel surcharges, port fees, and final-mile delivery.



Duties & Taxes
Country-specific import tariffs, custom agent fees, and local excise taxes.



Cargo Insurance
Premium paid to protect the shipment against loss, theft, or damage at sea.



Handling & Brokerage
Customs broker fees, documentation/bill of lading fees, and palletization.


3. Holding & Fulfillment (After Arrival)
Storage Costs
Warehouse rent, pallet storage fees, climate control, and security.



Pick and Pack
Fulfillment center labor to pick individual items and pack boxes.



Packaging Materials
Branded boxes, bubble wrap, tape, inserts, and shipping labels.



Inventory Carrying
Opportunity cost of tied-up capital and interest on inventory financing.


4. Post-Sale (After the Sale)
Customer Shipping
Outbound shipping fees to send the product to the end consumer.



Returns & Exchanges
Reverse logistics shipping, restocking labor, and unsellable damaged goods.



Shrinkage & Waste
Inventory lost to theft, expiration, obsolescence, or warehouse damage.

Everything in JavaScript relies on two core layers:

The UI Frameworks
These are frontend libraries that handle component rendering and state management. These replace raw HTML/JS with reactive components.

React: The most popular library, which uses JSX (mixing HTML inside JavaScript functions). It relies on explicit hooks (useState) to track updates.
Vue (or Vue.js): It uses Single-File Components (.vue files) separating HTML <template>, JS <script>, and CSS <style>.

title: Excluding Your Own Traffic
text:
Analytics on a site you built are answering the wrong question until your own visits are out of them. Development traffic is the worst offender: every local reload counts as a fresh visit, so the numbers report how often you rebuilt the site rather than whether anyone reads it.
There are three mechanisms. They are not equivalent, and the obvious one is the weakest.

title: Excluding Your Own Traffic
section: The IP filter — the obvious answer, and usually the wrong one
text:
The IP filter — the obvious answer, and usually the wrong one
GA4 has this built in. Admin → Data Streams → Configure tag settings → Define internal traffic creates a rule matching an IP and stamps traffic_type: internal on those hits. Admin → Data Settings → Data Filters then excludes them.
Two traps:

The filter ships as “Testing”, which filters nothing. It has to be switched to Active. A filter left in Testing looks configured and does not work.
It degrades silently. A residential IP rotates on the ISP’s schedule and a phone on cellular never matches. The rule keeps looking correct while quietly counting you again, and nothing notifies you.

It also cannot separate local development from ordinary browsing at home, since both come from the same address.
Treat an IP filter as a backstop on a static office IP, never as the primary mechanism.

title: Excluding Your Own Traffic
text:
Blocking versus tagging
Once the site knows it is you, it can either not send anything or send with traffic_type: 'internal' and let a GA4 filter exclude it.
Blocking is simpler, has fewer places to misconfigure, and does not send your browsing to Google at all. Tagging is reversible — flip the filter between Active and Testing to see reports with and without yourself — at the cost of splitting the logic across your code and a console setting.
If the mechanism is a guard that returns before the tag loads, the choice is already made: nothing has loaded, so there is nothing to tag.

title: Excluding Your Own Traffic
text:
Verifying it, including the control
Confirm against live GA4, not by reading the code:

Excluded context — load the site with the browser’s Network tab filtered to googletagmanager. Expect zero requests.
Included context — from a browser that is not excluded, browse with GA4 Realtime open. Your session should appear within about thirty seconds.

Step 2 is the one people skip and the only one that proves anything. An empty Realtime report is indistinguishable from analytics being broken outright — which is precisely the failure that quietly reports “nobody visits”.

title: Prefect
text:
Why use Prefect? and best practices.

1. Key Components of Data Pipeline Monitoring

Instrumentation: Generating logs to capture errors and emitting metrics to measure performance.
Collection & Storage: Aggregating logs and metrics from various sources (using agents, log trawling, or APIs like OpenTelemetry).
Observability: Centralizing data into a dashboard to track trends, inspect logs, and identify root causes quickly.
Alerting & Remediation: Setting metric thresholds that trigger manual notifications (e.g., to on-call staff) or automated fixes (e.g., auto-scaling clusters).




2. Best Practices

Avoid Monolithic Architecture: Modularize your pipeline into separate components (ingestion, transformation, storage, reporting). Monitoring each part independently isolates failures and prevents cascading errors.
Make Dependencies Explicit: Define and document precise inputs/outputs for each step. Use tools like Pydantic to validate data types before processing to catch errors early with clear messages.
Define Clear Metrics & Thresholds:
Consistency: Track completion success rates and allowable downtime between successful runs.
Timeliness: Monitor pipeline duration and latency to detect unusual slowdowns or premature stops.
Validity: Classify error types (e.g., expected API downtime vs. unexpected malformed data).
Centralize Logging and Alerting: Ship all logs and metrics to a single platform and tag runs (e.g., with UUIDs) to trace requests across multi-cloud or hybrid environments.
Use Reliable Monitoring Infrastructure: Avoid building complex custom monitoring tools that create additional single points of failure; leverage dedicated workflow orchestration platforms (like Prefect) instead.

title: Directory Structure
text:
The thing with using a tool is to get the grasp of the bigger picture. I like to know how the environment of the tool that I use usually looks like in dev / prod. I’m not well versed with how an actual backend directory structure should look like, but let’s start with something very simple. There seems to be two recommended ways: one for small to medium sized apps, and another for large apps. Let’s write down both to consider when making or working on projects.
To be honest, I don’t think I will be ever using the second type of structure, so just rely on the first structure.

title: Directory Structure
section: Structure 1: Organized by Layer (Best for Medium Apps)
text:
Structure 1: Organized by Layer (Best for Medium Apps)
This approach is popular for small-to-medium APIs. It separates your application logic by architectural responsibility (routes, business logic, and database).

my_fastapi_project/
├── alembic/                  # Database migration files (if using Alembic)
├── app/                      # Main application package
│   ├── api/                  # API layer (HTTP routers and endpoints)
│   │   ├── v1/
│   │   │   ├── auth.py
│   │   │   └── users.py
│   │   └── deps.py           # Common FastAPI dependencies (e.g., get_db, get_current_user)
│   ├── core/                 # Application configuration & security setup
│   │   ├── config.py         # Pydantic Settings for environment variables
│   │   └── security.py       # Password hashing and JWT generation
│   ├── crud/                 # Raw database interactions (Create, Read, Update, Delete)

text: Which command to run, how to shape it, and where a flag is allowed to live. Which nodes the command touches is Node Selection.

title: Workflow
text:
Command Shape

dbt <subcommand> [flags]

Flags go after the subcommand. Putting them before it (dbt --fail-fast run) is legacy behaviour dbt Labs can drop at any release, and the same flag on both sides is unsupported.









Flag kind
Shape
Example




boolean
--<config> / --no-<config>
dbt run --fail-fast, dbt run --no-fail-fast


non-boolean
--<config>=<setting>
dbt test --indirect-selection=cautious

title: Workflow
text:
Commands




Command
What it does




dbt debug
validates the connection, profile, and project config


dbt clean
deletes everything in clean-targets (target/, dbt_packages/)


dbt deps
installs the packages pinned in packages.yml


dbt seed
loads the CSVs in seeds/


dbt run
materializes models only — no tests, seeds, or snapshots


dbt test
runs data tests and unit tests


dbt snapshot
runs snapshots


dbt build
seed + run + test + snapshot in dependency order, per node


dbt compile
renders jinja to target/compiled/, runs nothing


dbt ls
prints the nodes a selector resolves to, runs nothing


dbt source freshness
checks source loaded_at and writes sources.json


dbt docs generate
builds the catalog, see Documentation




dbt build is the default reach. It interleaves tests with runs node by node, so a failing test stops the downstream models instead of letting them build on bad data.

title: Workflow
text:
Flags
Ordered by how often I actually reach for them.




Flag
Short
What it does




--target
-t
which profiles.yml output to run against


--select
-s
which nodes to run — see Node Selection


--exclude

remove nodes from the --select set


--fail-fast
-x
stop on the first failure instead of finishing the run


--full-refresh
-f
rebuild incremental models from scratch as tables


--empty

schema-only dry run: refs and sources limited to zero rows


--state

path to a comparison manifest, for state: and --defer


--defer

resolve unbuilt refs against --state instead of the target


--store-failures

write failing test rows to a table instead of discarding them


--warn-error

treat every warning as an error


--threads

override the thread count from profiles.yml





--full-refresh
Reach for it when an incremental model’s schema changed, or when its logic changed and the existing rows are now wrong. It makes is_incremental() return false for every model in the invocation, so scope it with --select:

dbt run --select "fct_orders" --full-refresh

Incremental strategy itself is in Materializations & Build Time.


--empty
Executes the model SQL against the warehouse with zero-row inputs. Validates that the DAG compiles and the models build, without paying for the scan. This is the cheap pre-flight before a full run.

dbt build --empty --select "state:modified+" --state prod-artifacts/

title: Workflow
text:
Where a Flag Lives
Same flag, four possible homes. Most specific wins:

CLI option  >  environment variable  >  dbt_project.yml flags:  >  ~/.dbt/user_settings.yml  >  dbt default









Home
Use it for




CLI option
behaviour specific to this invocation


environment variable
behaviour that differs per environment — dev, prod, CI


flags: in dbt_project.yml
version-controlled defaults for everyone on the project


~/.dbt/user_settings.yml
personal preference across every project on this machine





# dbt_project.yml
flags:
  fail_fast: true


export DBT_ENGINE_FAIL_FAST=1   # env var
dbt run --no-fail-fast          # CLI wins over both







The env var prefix changed



v1.11 and later use DBT_ENGINE_. v1.10 and earlier used plain DBT_. Anything copied off an older blog post or an old CI file is setting a variable dbt no longer reads, silently.


Two exceptions to the four homes:

Path flags (--state, --log-path, --target-path) cannot go in dbt_project.yml. CLI or env var (DBT_ENGINE_STATE, DBT_ENGINE_LOG_PATH) only. Path configs that tell dbt where project resources live — model-paths, seed-paths — are different: they are static top-level keys in dbt_project.yml, outside the flags: dict.
Behaviour-change opt-ins can only go in dbt_project.yml, so the migration is reviewed in a pull request rather than diverging per machine.

Jinja can read a flag through the flags context variable, upper-cased:

# dbt_project.yml
on-run-start:
  - '{{ log("stopping at the first failure", info = true) if flags.FAIL_FAST }}'

title: Tests
text: The four kinds of data test and where each one is declared are in Naming. This page is about what we actually test for.

title: Tests
text:
Generic Tests
Declared inline in _{layer}__models.yml, on the column they apply to. unique and not_null on every primary key, relationships on every foreign key, accepted_values on anything enum-like that staging categorized. The yaml formatting for these is in Styling.

title: Tests
text:
Singular Tests
The tests that go under the dbt_project/tests/ is for conservation tests (at least that’s what I do).

Test Distinct Dimensional Integrity (row counts)

test for expected number of rows against actual number of rows

Test Metric Invariance (aggregate conservation)

test for expected agg against actual agg


Both are inter-intra layer checks: the point is that a row or a sum that existed in staging still exists, unchanged, once it reaches a mart. Generic tests cannot express that, which is what makes these singular.
Named assert_{domain}__{condition}.sql.

title: Tests
text:
Where Tests Run
dbt build interleaves tests with the models they belong to, so a failed test stops the downstream build instead of letting it run on bad data. See Workflow.

title: Marts
text: Gold. Star or snowflake schema, modeled for the business rather than for the pipeline.

title: Marts
text:
Allowed

dimension, fact, and bridge tables
BI and semantic models, materialized as views on top of the tables
joins and unions, both intra and inter model

title: Marts
text:
Not Allowed

staging-grade cleanup. anything that is a rename or a cast should have happened three layers ago
one-off reporting logic that only a single dashboard needs

The mart table types, and when to reach for each, are covered in Types of Mart Tables.

title: Marts
text:
Naming
{dim|fct|bridge}_{domain}__{entity}.sql, entity plural. There is no marts_ prefix — the layer is expressed by which of the three the model is. Full grammar in Naming.

title: Staging
text: Bronze. Maps the raw source onto standard business entities so that nothing downstream has to think about how the source happened to shape its data.

title: Staging
text:
Allowed

rename columns
type cast columns
basic computations, mostly for conversions or type casting
categorizing (enums, booleans)
variant / semi-structured normalization
map source table names to standard business entities
joins and unions within the same source, which normalizing variant columns sometimes needs

title: Staging
text:
Not Allowed

business logic of any kind, that is Intermediate’s job
joins or unions across sources
dropping source detail. staging keeps every single detail and data from the raw source

title: Staging
text:
Naming
stg_{source}__{entity}.sql, entity plural. The domain slot holds the source, not the domain — this is the one layer where that is true. Full grammar in Naming.

title: Staging
text:
Renaming a Reserved Word
When the source column is a reserved word, alias it once, in the import CTE, rather than at each point of use:

with character_ability as (

    select
        *,
        date as snapshot_date

    from {{ source('nexon', 'character_ability') }}

),

The import CTE then carries both names, so every downstream reference works unchanged — bare, table-qualified, and using (snapshot_date, ocid) alike. Aliasing at the point of use instead means deciding, CTE by CTE, whether this one reads the raw import (needs date as snapshot_date) or an already-renamed CTE (needs plain snapshot_date), and getting it wrong in one branch of a union all breaks the build. The duplicate lives inside the import CTE only: every other CTE selects explicit columns, so the model output carries just the new name.
Only staging can do this, because only staging’s import CTE is allowed select *.

title: Staging
text:
Casting Source Booleans
Check the value domain before you cast. A column named *_flag is not necessarily a boolean:

select col, count(*) from {{ source(...) }} group by 1;

Postgres accepts 0, 1, true, and false from text, so those cast straight with ::boolean. Localized labels do not — a Korean API happily returns 미적용 / 미사용 / 가능 / 비인간형 in a field whose name ends in _flag. Those need a case.
When only one of the two values appears in the data you have, do not guess the counterpart string:

case
    when x is null then null
    when x = '미적용' then false
    else true
end as has_golden_hammer

This stays correct whatever the unseen value turns out to be, as long as the field is two-valued. Mapping the observed value and leaving else null silently nulls out every row of the other kind instead.
Check for empty strings too. ''::boolean errors where null::boolean is fine, so confirm the blanks are real NULLs before a cast reaches production data.

title: Staging
text:
Materialization
View. Set project-wide under models.{project}.{domain}.staging in dbt_project.yml, see Project Structure.

title: Staging
text:
Column Order
Group and label columns by data type:

ids -> strings -> numerics -> booleans -> dates -> timestamps

This ordering holds in every layer, not just staging. The worked example is in Styling.

title: Staging
text:
Tests & Contracts

a data contract applies to this layer
_stg__sources.yml declares the source database and schema plus a brief documentation of the origin of the data
_stg__models.yml declares models, columns, data tests, and descriptions

title: Staging
text:
Shape
The source + renamed two-CTE pattern, written out in full in Styling. Staging is the only place where select * off a { source() } is allowed, because the layer is supposed to see every raw column — see Materializations & Build Time for why every other import CTE prunes instead.

title: Styling
text: Style rules taken from dbt Labs’ how we style our dbt projects guide. These apply to every layer, not just staging. Python model styling is left out since we don’t use Python models.

title: Styling
text:
Model and Field Names

model names are plural: customers, orders, products. the full file naming grammar is in Naming
every model has a primary key
primary key is named {object}_id, like account_id, so it’s obvious which id is referenced downstream
keys are string data types
use underscores in model names, never dots

most platforms use dots to separate database.schema.object, so underscores avoid quoting issues

same field name across models. a key to customers is customer_id, not user_id or id
no abbreviations or aliases. customer not cust, orders not o
avoid reserved words as column names. the aliasing trick for a source column that is one is in Staging
booleans prefixed with is_ or has_, and never also suffixed _flag. is_ for state, has_ for possession: is_accessed, is_ongoing, has_golden_hammer

a source _flag column keeps the prefix at the front of the whole name, ahead of any {parent}__{child} nesting: boss_contents__complete_flag becomes is_boss_contents__completed
the rule assumes the column really is a boolean. how to check and cast is in Staging

timestamps named {event}_at in UTC. non-UTC gets a suffix, like created_at_pt

our project is KST so we use the _kst suffix

dates named {event}_date
event dates and times in past tense: created, updated, deleted
price and revenue fields in decimal currency (19.99 for $19.99). if kept as integer cents, suffix it as price_in_cents
schema, table, and column names in snake_case
names based on business terminology, not source terminology. if the source says user_id but the business says customer, use customer_id
model versions use a _v1, _v2 suffix
consistent ordering of data types, grouped and labeled by type. same order in every layer, not only staging

ids -> strings -> numerics -> booleans -> dates -> timestamps



with

source as (

    select * from {{ source('ecom', 'raw_orders') }}

),

renamed as (

    select

        ----------  ids
        id as order_id,
        store_id as location_id,
        customer as customer_id,

        ---------- strings
        status as order_status,

        ---------- numerics
        (order_total / 100.0)::float as order_total,
        (tax_paid / 100.0)::float as tax_paid,

        ---------- booleans
        is_fulfilled,

        ---------- dates
        date(order_date) as ordered_date,

        ---------- timestamps
        ordered_at

    from source

)

select * from renamed







Note



The source + renamed shape above is a staging pattern. Intermediate and mart models use ref() and joins instead, but the naming and column ordering rules still hold.

title: Styling
text:
SQL Basics

no select *, with exactly two exceptions

the last line of a model, select * from {final_cte}
a staging import CTE reading off a { source() }, as in the example above, because staging is supposed to carry every raw column forward. an import CTE reading off a { ref() } never gets this — see Materializations & Build Time

all lower case for field names, keywords, and function names
trailing commas
four space indents
lines no longer than 80 characters
as written explicitly when aliasing a field or table
jinja comments ({# #}) for comments that shouldn’t end up in the compiled SQL
sqlfluff enforces all of this automatically

customize .sqlfluff to the project
exclude target/, dbt_packages/, and macros/ with a .sqlfluffignore to speed up linting

title: Styling
text:
Fields and Aggregations

fields stated before aggregates and window functions
aggregate as early as possible, on the smallest data set, before joining
group and order by number (group by 1, 2) instead of listing column names

if grouping by more than a few columns, the model design needs another look

title: Styling
text:
Joins

prefer union all over union unless you actually want duplicates removed
when joining two or more tables, always prefix column names with the table name. single table selects don’t need it
be explicit about the join type. inner join, not join
no table aliases in join conditions, especially initialisms. customers beats c
always move left to right. a right join usually means you should swap which table you select from and which you join to

title: Styling
text:
Import CTEs

all { ref('...') } statements go in CTEs at the top of the file
import CTEs are named after the table they reference
limit the data scanned. select only the columns used and filter with where


with

orders as (

    select
        order_id,
        customer_id,
        order_total,
        order_date

    from {{ ref('orders') }}

    where order_date >= '2020-01-01'

)

title: Styling
text:
Functional CTEs

where performance permits, a CTE does a single logical unit of work
CTE names are as verbose as needed to convey what they do. events_joined_to_users, not user_events, which is a model name, not a transformation
CTEs duplicated across models get pulled out into their own intermediate models
last line of a model is select * from the final CTE, so you can swap in an earlier CTE to audit intermediate output while developing

title: Styling
Styling
text:
Example SQL

with

my_data as (

    select
        field_1,
        field_2,
        field_3,
        cancellation_date,
        expiration_date,
        start_date

    from {{ ref('my_data') }}

),

some_cte as (

    select
        id,
        field_4,
        field_5

    from {{ ref('some_cte') }}

),

some_cte_agg as (

    select
        id,
        sum(field_4) as total_field_4,
        max(field_5) as max_field_5

    from some_cte

    group by 1

),

{# CTE comments go here #}
joined as (

    select
        my_data.field_1,
        my_data.field_2,
        my_data.field_3,

        -- use line breaks to visually separate calculations into blocks
        case
            when my_data.cancellation_date is null
                and my_data.expiration_date is not null
                then expiration_date
            when my_data.cancellation_date is null
                then my_data.start_date + 7
            else my_data.cancellation_date
        end as cancellation_date,

        some_cte_agg.total_field_4,
        some_cte_agg.max_field_5

    from my_data

    left join some_cte_agg
        on my_data.id = some_cte_agg.id

    where my_data.field_1 = 'abc' and
        (
            my_data.field_2 = 'def' or
            my_data.field_2 = 'ghi'
        )

    having count(*) > 1

)

select * from joined

title: Styling
Styling
text:
YAML

two space indents
list items are indented
a single entry list can be a string like 'select': 'other_user', but an explicit list is better: 'select': ['other_user']
new line between list items that are dictionaries
lines no longer than 80 characters
the dbt json schema plus prettier validates and formats these automatically


models:
  - name: events
    columns:
      - name: event_id
        description: This is a unique identifier for the event
        data_tests:
          - unique
          - not_null

      - name: event_time
        description: "When the event occurred in UTC (eg. 2018-01-01 12:00:00)"
        data_tests:
          - not_null

      - name: user_id
        description: The ID of the user who recorded the event
        data_tests:
          - not_null
          - relationships:
              arguments: # available in v1.10.5 and higher
                to: ref('users')
                field: id

title: Styling
text:
Enforcing Style

pre-commit hooks catch and often auto-fix violations before the commit lands. dbt-checkpoint is the dbt specific hook set

add this only after the codebase already conforms, otherwise every commit fails

dbt_project_evaluator flags where the project deviates from dbt best practices and recommends fixes. covers modeling, testing, documentation, structure, performance, and governance

title: Project Structure
text: This page covers the shape of the project on disk and the three meta files that configure it. Naming rules for the files inside models/ live in Naming.

title: Project Structure
text:
Project Directory Structure
Let’s first get a grasp of the bigger picture by looking at how the full directory structure looks like:

dbt_project/
├── .dbt/                              # Profiles dir (optional, project-local)
│   └── profiles.yml                   # Connection profiles (git-ignored)
├── analyses/                          # Ad-hoc analytical queries (not materialized)
├── dbt_packages/                      # Installed packages (git-ignored)
├── logs/                              # Run logs (git-ignored)
├── macros/                            # Custom macros & generic tests
│   └── generate_schema_name.sql
├── models/
│   └── {domain}/
│       ├── staging/
│       │   ├── _stg__sources.yml     # Source db/schema + origin docs
│       │   ├── _stg__models.yml      # Models, columns, tests, descriptions
│       │   └── stg_{source}__{entity}.sql
│       ├── intermediate/
│       │   ├── _int__models.yml
│       │   └── int_{domain}__{entity}.sql
│       └── marts/
│           ├── _marts__models.yml
│           └── {dim|fct|bridge}_{domain}__{entity}.sql
├── seeds/                             # Static CSV reference data
├── snapshots/                         # SCD type-2 snapshots
├── target/                            # Compiled SQL & artifacts (git-ignored)
├── tests/                             # Singular (complex) data tests
│   └── assert_{domain}__{condition}.sql
├── .env                               # Env vars (git-ignored, see the warning below)
├── .gitignore
├── dbt_project.yml                    # Project config
└── packages.yml                       # Package dependencies

Below we’ll discuss what each component is and how to fill them in.






Note



If there is only one domain, there is no need to nest the staging, intermediate, and marts layer. Just simply go with models/{staging|intermediate|marts}.

title: Project Structure
text:
Project Level Meta Files

dbt_project.yml

name: '{project_name}'
version: '{version}'
config-version: 2

profile: '{project_name}'

model-paths: ['models']
analysis-paths: ['analyses']
test-paths: ['tests']
seed-paths: ['seeds']
macro-paths: ['macros']
snapshot-paths: ['snapshots']

target-path: "target"
clean-targets:
  - 'target'
  - 'dbt_packages'

models:
  +persist_docs:
    relation: true
    columns: true
  {project_name}:
    {domain}: # repeat this block per domain (optional)
      +schema: {SCHEMA}
      +grants: # domain-level default grants (optional)
        {privilege}: ['{ROLE}'] # e.g. select, references
      staging:
        +materialized: view
        +database: {STAGE_DB}
        +docs:
          node_color: "#CD7F32" # bronze color
      intermediate:
        +materialized: view # or table when heavy
        +database: {STAGE_DB}
        +docs:
          node_color: "#A0A0A0" # silver color
      marts:
        +materialized: table
        +database: {MART_DB}
        +docs:
          node_color: "#FFD700" # gold color
        +grants: # optional: override domain grants for marts
          {privilege}: ['{ROLE}', '{ROLE}'] # e.g. select, references
        +tags: ['{tag}'] # optional

seeds:
  {project_name}:
    +database: {STAGE_DB}
    {domain}: # repeat this block per domain
      +schema: {SCHEMA}
      +quote_columns: true # optional
      +docs:
        node_color: "#008000" # green color
      +grants: # optional
        {privilege}: ['{ROLE}'] # e.g. select, references



packages.yml

packages:
    - package: dbt-labs/dbt_utils
      version: 1.3.2
    - package: godatadriven/dbt_date
      version: 0.17.0
    - package: Snowflake-Labs/dbt_semantic_view
      version: 1.0.3



profiles.yml

PostgresSnowflake



{project_name}:
  target: dev
  outputs:
    dev:
      type: {adapter_type}
      host: "{{ env_var('host') }}"
      user: "{{ env_var('user') }}"
      password: "{{ env_var('password') }}"

generate_schema_name
The outputs above differ in database and nothing else. That is deliberate: the
environment is the database, the schema is the layer, so a schema name is
identical in every environment and nothing downstream carries the environment as
a string. Every source, every ref, and every hand-written query against the
warehouse stays byte-identical between targets, and switching environment is a
change of connection only.
The macro therefore has nothing to add to the name — but it still has to exist,
because dbt’s default prefixes the custom schema with the profile’s schema:
and would build public_staging:

{% macro generate_schema_name(custom_schema_name, node) -%}
    {%- if custom_schema_name is not none -%}
        {{ custom_schema_name | trim }}
    {%- elif node is not none and node.resource_type == 'model' -%}
        {{ exceptions.raise_compiler_error(
            "No +schema configured for model '" ~ node.name ~ "'"
        ) }}
    {%- else -%}
        {{ target.schema | trim }}
    {%- endif -%}
{%- endmacro %}

Two details in that body:

Raise only for models. dbt resolves a schema for every node it parses, and
tests carry no +schema: of their own, so raising unconditionally breaks
dbt test. The else branch is what tests land on.
Raising at all is worth it: a model whose directory has no matching models:
block in dbt_project.yml otherwise builds silently into the profile’s
schema, which is the kind of thing you find weeks later.

The alternative — one database, schemas prefixed dev_ / prod_ — reads worse
(dev_stage.dev_staging) and puts the environment into every source definition.
The only thing it buys is cross-environment queries in one connection, which on
Postgres is impossible anyway.

Deeper nesting
The pattern recurses. A list inside qux (e.g. qux[].items) creates foo__qux__items, whose _dlt_parent_id points at the foo__qux row. Each extra __<name> on a table = one more level of list nesting.

GitHub
Go to https://github.com/ and create an account.

SSH key Authentication
This is a key-pair authentication. SSH authentication uses a pair of keys that work like a lock and key:

Private Key (id_ed25519): Stays strictly on your computer. Never share this.
Public Key (id_ed25519.pub): Acts as the lock that only your private key can open. Upload this to GitHub.


Step 1: Generate a new SSH key pair

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your.email@example.com"

Some prompts will appear asking:

where to save they keys, press Enter to accept the default location (~./ssh).
for a passphrase, press Enter to leave it empty (convenient), or type a password for extra security.







Note



If you decide to enter a passphrase, be aware that the terminal will not show any visual feedback (such as asterisks or characters) while you are typing. Simply type the passphrase fully and press Enter.




Step 2: Add the SSH Key to the ssh-agent
The ssh-agent is what manages your keys in the background.

Start the agent:


eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"


Add your private key to the agent:


ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519



Step 3: Add the Public Key to GitHub

Copy the public key’s content to your clipboard:


pbcopy < ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub


Go to GitHub, click your profile picture (top-right corner), and then Settings.
In the left sidebar, click SSH and GPG keys.
Click New SSH key (green button top-right).
Give it a descriptive title of your local machine (e.g., “my-mac”) and paste your key from the clip board.
Click Add SSH key.



Step 4: Test the Connection

ssh -T git git@github.com

If you see a message like the following, then you are good to go.

Hi {username}! You've successfully authenticated, but GitHub does not provide shell access.







Note



This authenticates one account. For a machine that needs a second
(work alongside personal), see Multiple Accounts.

Homebrew is a package manager for macOS that lets you easily install, update, and manage software tools and applications through the terminal using simple CLI commands.
It is divided into three main components:

Formulae (Formulas): Package definitions for command-line tools (e.g., brew install python or brew install wget).
Casks: Extensions that let you install full macOS desktop applications, fonts, and plugins (e.g., brew install –cask google-chrome or brew install –cask visual-studio-code).

Formulas and casks are what’s installed and the cellar is where it’s stored.

title: Merge Strategies
text:
Three buttons sit on a GitHub pull request, and they do genuinely different
things to history. Picking one is a decision you make once per repository, so it
is worth understanding what each leaves behind.

title: Merge Strategies
section: The one Git has that GitHub does not
text:
The one Git has that GitHub does not
A fast-forward creates nothing. main is just a pointer, and if every commit
on main is already an ancestor of the branch, merging means sliding that
pointer forward.





gitGraph
    commit id: "A"
    commit id: "B"
    branch feature
    checkout feature
    commit id: "C"
    commit id: "D"
    checkout main
    merge feature id: "pointer moves"







git checkout main && git merge --ff-only feature

C and D keep their exact SHAs, author dates, committer dates and signatures.
main and feature end up pointing at the identical commit. If main has moved
on at all, git refuses rather than inventing anything — that refusal is the
feature.






Important



GitHub has no fast-forward button. Not in the merge UI, not in gh pr merge. A true fast-forward can only be done locally and pushed. Every GitHub
merge strategy creates new commits.

title: Merge Strategies
text:
The three GitHub offers

Merge commit
Keeps every commit and adds one more that joins the two lines.





gitGraph
    commit id: "A"
    branch feature
    checkout feature
    commit id: "C"
    commit id: "D"
    checkout main
    commit id: "B"
    merge feature id: "merge commit"






History is a truthful record of what happened in parallel, and it is a thicket
to read. git log --graph becomes necessary rather than optional. Common on
older repositories and on release-branch models.


Squash and merge
Collapses the whole branch into one new commit on main.





gitGraph
    commit id: "A"
    commit id: "B"
    commit id: "squashed PR"






One commit per pull request. The branch’s individual commits are discarded —
they survive only on the closed PR page. This is the most common default at
companies, because it makes main a clean list of shipped changes and it
means nobody has to care how messy a branch was mid-review.
The consequence worth internalising: the PR title and body become the commit
message. Writing a good PR description is not politeness, it is the permanent
record.


Rebase and merge
Replays each commit from the branch onto the tip of main, one at a time.





gitGraph
    commit id: "A"
    commit id: "B"
    commit id: "C'"
    commit id: "D'"






Linear like a fast-forward, and every commit survives individually. But C' and
D' are copies: same content, new SHAs, new committer dates. The originals
are left orphaned on your local branch.

title: Merge Strategies
section: What a rewrite does to your local branch
text:
What a rewrite does to your local branch
After a rebase or squash merge, your local branch and main hold identical
content under different commits. Git reports this as divergence:

$ git diff dev origin/main          # empty — content is the same
$ git rev-list --count origin/main..dev   # 41
$ git rev-list --count dev..origin/main   # 41

Forty-one commits “ahead” and forty-one “behind” with no actual difference. Each
of your commits has a twin on main that git cannot recognise as the same
thing.






Warning



Never git merge to fix this. Merging replays all your originals on top of
their own copies and duplicates the entire branch.


Allowed

git checkout dev && git reset --hard origin/main

Not allowed

git checkout dev && git merge origin/main     # duplicates every commit

The cleaner habit avoids the problem entirely: let the branch die at the
merge. Branch per change, delete it after, branch again from a fresh main.
Divergence cannot happen to a branch that no longer exists.

git checkout main && git pull
git checkout -b fix/some-thing
# work, commit, push, open PR, merge in the browser
git checkout main && git pull
git branch -d fix/some-thing

Set Automatically delete head branches in repository settings and GitHub
deletes the remote side for you.

Anything derived from a commit date
A rewrite moves the committer date and leaves the author date alone.




Format
Meaning
Survives a rebase




%aI
when the change was written
yes


%cI
when the commit object was last created
no




Any script reading git log -1 --format=%cI will see every commit in a merged

text:
What I do here
Repository settings restrict this to rebase only — merge commits and squash
are switched off, so the wrong button cannot be clicked by accident.
Rebase over squash because commits here are written to stand alone, and squash
would flatten a deliberately separated set into one. Rebase over a local
fast-forward because merging in the browser is what collaboration looks like,
and the practice is worth more than exact SHAs on a personal repository.
The accepted costs: SHAs are rewritten, the local branch needs reset --hard
after each merge, and anything reading %cI churns once per merge.

merging and Require linear history. This is what stops a habitual push
straight to main.

title: Chezmoi
text: Chezmoi is a dotfiles manager that keeps your configuration files (.zshrc, .gitconfig, kitty config, etc.) in a single git repository and syncs them across machines. Instead of manually copying config files to a new machine or symlinking them one by one, you keep a source repo and let chezmoi write the files into $HOME for you.

title: Chezmoi
text:
Mental Model
There are two trees to keep in mind:

Source: the git repository where your dotfiles live, chezmoi repo. This is what you commit and push.
Target: $HOME. This is what chezmoi writes out.

The flow to push and pull your files:

chezmoi apply pushes source → target
chezmoi add|re-add pulls target → source






graph LR
    B["Target<br>$HOME"]
    A["Source<br>~/path/to/your/chezmoi"]
    A -->|chezmoi apply| B
    B -->|chezmoi add #124; re-add| A

title: Chezmoi
text:
Installation

brew install chezmoi

title: Chezmoi
text:
Setup
By default chezmoi looks for source files in ~/.local/share/chezmoi. If you want to keep your dotfiles repo somewhere else (e.g. alongside your other projects), you need to tell chezmoi where to look.
Create ~/.config/chezmoi/chezmoi.toml, substituting your actual path:

sourceDir = "~/path/to/your/chezmoi"







Note



Should we save the chezmoi.toml file?
Chicken-and-egg problem
This config file can itself be tracked by the repo (at dot_config/chezmoi/chezmoi.toml), but you still have to create it by hand the first time, because chezmoi has to read it before it knows where the source directory is. After the initial chezmoi apply, chezmoi takes over and any future edits go through the source tree like everything else. However, I wouldn’t personally recommend it.


Verify it’s wired up:

chezmoi source-path
# → /path/to/your/chezmoi

Then preview and apply. Always diff before applying on a new machine as the source tree may contain files that would overwrite something already in $HOME:

chezmoi diff      # show changes against $HOME
chezmoi apply     # write to $HOME (overwrite)







Warning



Chezmoi tries to apply everything in the source tree to $HOME, not just files prefixed with dot_. Anything that isn’t a dotfile source (e.g. README.md, docs/) will be copied into $HOME verbatim unless it’s listed in .chezmoiignore. When adding non-dotfile content to the repo, add it to .chezmoiignore, and sanity-check with chezmoi managed.

title: Chezmoi
text:
Workflow

Common commands

chezmoi cd                # drop into the source dir (the repo)
chezmoi diff              # show what apply would change in $HOME
chezmoi apply             # write chezmoi → $HOME
chezmoi add ~/.file       # start tracking a file (copy $HOME → chezmoi)
chezmoi re-add ~/.file    # pull edits made in $HOME back into chezmoi
chezmoi status            # short status of pending changes
chezmoi managed           # list every file chezmoi manages



Adding a new dotfile
To start tracking a file that currently only lives in $HOME:

chezmoi add ~/.some-config

Chezmoi copies it into the source tree, renaming it to its internal convention (e.g. .some-config → dot_some-config). Commit the new file from inside the repo.


Editing a tracked file
The recommended way to edit the tracked file is to edit the source by doing chezmoi edit ~/.some-config. However, I prefer to just edit the live file as I don’t want to change the way I used to manage my files before chezmoi. Also, some configurations are changed automatically by tools (e.g. a binary setting paths to a zsh script) and the chezmoi recommended way can add overhead (e.g. changing a config in the native settings panel of an editor like VS Code or Obsidian but having to go to chezmoi to change it instead of inside the editor).
That’s why I just edit my tracked files manually in my editor of choice, VS Code, if it’s a file that can be opened and edited.
Then follow the steps:

Re-add the changes to track it with chezmoi:


chezmoi re-add ~/.edited-config # or just chezmoi re-add


Check the differences in your editor of choice.
Take action to save or revert.

if you like the changes: git commit.
if you don’t like the changes: revert changes and chezmoi apply to overwrite $HOME with the reverted version (before the edits).








Tip



Always do the chezmoi re-add first, as the chezmoi directory is being tracked, so it’s okay to be overwritten. You can review the changes in an editor and commit only what’s necessary. However, your $HOME is not git tracked, so if you do a chezmoi apply first, it overwrites your live files and the previous version is gone.




Syncing across machines
On the machine where you made changes:

chezmoi cd
git add -p && git commit -m "..."
git push

On the other machine:

chezmoi cd
git pull
chezmoi diff      # sanity-check
chezmoi apply



Scoping an apply
chezmoi apply with no arguments walks the whole tree, and it stops at the first
target that changed on disk since chezmoi last wrote it — asking what to do. In a
non-interactive shell (an agent, a script, CI) there is no TTY to answer with, so
it fails outright:

.claude/statusline-command.sh has changed since chezmoi last wrote it?
chezmoi: could not open a new TTY: open /dev/tty: device not configured

Nothing after that point gets applied. Pass explicit target paths so unrelated
drift can’t block the files you actually changed:

chezmoi apply ~/.zshenv ~/.zprofile ~/.zshrc
chezmoi diff ~/.zshenv ~/.zprofile ~/.zshrc   # empty output = in sync

Scoping is also the safer habit generally: it makes the blast radius of an apply
exactly the files you name, instead of everything the source tree happens to hold.

There are a lot of different workflows.
Git related workflows differ per person and community be it an open-source project or company.
The two that are well recognized like paradigms are Git Flow and GitHub Flow.
I think the Git Flow is too complex for me so I will go with GitHub Flow. That is not because one is better than the other but you have to consider the size of your project and don’t over complicate stuff.

    merge release id: "release" tag: "v1.0"
    checkout develop
    merge release id: "back to dev"
    checkout main

    checkout hotfix
    commit id: "urgent fix"
    checkout main
    merge hotfix id: "hotfix" tag: "v1.0.1"
    checkout develop

I will not go over the details as I’ve not used this flow so I’m no expert. Might cover it in the future if I get to work on more complex and big projects.

gitGraph

    commit id: "work"
    commit id: "more work"
    commit id: "review fixes"
    checkout main
    merge feature id: "PR merged" tag: "deploy"

The five steps, in words:

Branch: make a feature branch off main.
Commit: do the work, one commit at a time.
Pull Request: open a PR. Review is a loop, you assign a reviewer for feedback and fix if needed. Repeat until approved.
Merge: merge the PR back into main.
Deploy: main ships.

These five steps are all there is. This is quite simple and works for a solo or small dev team.

title: Workflow
text:
Choose a merge strategy
GitHub offers merge commit, squash and rebase — and deliberately not
fast-forward, which only exists locally. Which one you pick decides whether your
commits survive as themselves, get copied, or get collapsed.
I use rebase, enforced in repository settings. The reasoning, the trade-offs
and how to recover the local branch afterwards are in
Merge Strategies.

title: Workflow
text:
Workflow Details
The loop, in the order it actually happens.

Before touching anything

git status

Uncommitted work from last time is the usual surprise. Either finish it and
commit, or throw it away — do not start a new change on top of a dirty tree.
Needing to switch branches with work in progress is what stash is for:

git stash                 # park it
git checkout other-branch
git checkout -            # come back
git stash pop             # take it back



Branch
Off a fresh main, never off yesterday’s branch.

git checkout main && git pull
git checkout -b feature/short-description

Naming rules live in Conventions.


Commit
Small and often. One commit should be one reason, so that a reviewer can read
them in order and so that a bad one can be reverted alone.


Pull Request

git push -u origin feature/short-description
gh pr create

The description is the part people skip and the part that matters. A reviewer
arrives knowing nothing, so it needs what changed, why, and how it was
verified. On a squash-merge repository this text becomes the permanent commit
message, so it outlives the PR page.
Assign a reviewer. Review is a loop: comments, fixes, push again, repeat until
approved. Pushing to the same branch updates the PR automatically — no new PR.


Merge
Merge in the browser. Then bring the local side back and delete the branch:

git checkout main && git pull
git branch -d feature/short-description







Warning



After a rebase or squash merge the old branch has diverged from main even
though the content is identical. Delete it, or reset --hard it. Never merge
main back into it — see Merge Strategies.




Then start again
New branch off main for the next change. The branch is disposable; main is
the only long-lived thing.

title: RBAC
text:
ACCOUNTADMIN (Top-level, use sparingly)



- Should do: Account-level settings, billing/credit management, cross-region config, CREATE SNOWFLAKE INTELLIGENCE, enabling features.
- Should NOT do: Create day-to-day objects (databases, tables, warehouses), run automated scripts.
Best practice: Assign to 2+ users, require MFA, never set as anyone’s default role.








SECURITYADMIN (Grants & Security)



- Creates/manages: Privilege grants on all objects (has MANAGE GRANTS), role-to-role grants, role-to-user grants.
- Inherits: USERADMIN. Use for: GRANT ... TO ROLE, future grants, managed access schema grants.








USERADMIN (Users & Roles)



- Creates: Users (CREATE USER) and roles (CREATE ROLE).
- Use for: Provisioning new users, creating custom access/functional roles.








SYSADMIN (Infrastructure & Objects)



- Creates: Warehouses, databases, schemas, and all database objects.
- Clarification: While SYSADMIN can create these, any role with CREATE privileges can too.
- Best practice: All custom roles (like those used by dbt) must roll up to SYSADMIN so it inherits ownership and can manage all objects in the account.

title: Personal Knowledge Management
text:
I’ve tried a lot of different ways to manage my knowledge. I spent at least years trying to figure out what works best for me. Frameworks that other people have set, not me. However, I think that everyone has different ways to solve problems and different ways to study that suit them best.
I like simplicity and minimalism, but tend to get overwhelmed easily and just make a mess. After years of trying different tools and frameworks, finally I’ve settled down to making my own workflow and this feels way too comfortable. Not to mention that I’m still migrating everything and I’ve come to realize what a huge mess I’ve made along the way.
The frameworks that I’ve tried until now were: MOC, PARA, Zettelkasten, respectively. These were either way too structured (PARA) or way too unstructured (Zettelkasten) or just tedious to manage (MOC), for me. Also, if moved from different platforms like Apple Notes -> Notion -> Obsidian -> Notion -> Obsidian. The reason I chose Obsidian is that the more I got into coding and the advancement of AI, it’s way easier to manage markdown files and I like the native Obsidian plugins, which solve most of the pain points I’ve had while using Notion (it’s the platform I’ve used the longest and customized the most).






Note



Yes, the system I’ve built is also structured like PARA, but accustomed to my needs not something pre configured. While, Zettelkasten seems like a cool system, a big downside is that it’s hard to share with others meaning that it’s also hard to share with a future me.


That’s why I’ve chosen my own build to manage my knowledge. My personal workflow came to a more mature stage as I was making this personal website. And it is a mesh of MOC, PARA, and Zettelkasten along with some Obsidian native plugins like the BASE and CANVAS.
The architecture/structure consists of the following:

/archive

This is the directory that is for anything that doesn’t seem to belong in any of the other directories.

/blog

This is a directory for ideas that are shareable with the public.

/clippings

This is for Obsidian clipping through a chrome extension to save articles that are worthy of being absorbed by my notes.

/inbox

This is for sudden ideas that pop up and are mostly AI responses to structure my questions.

/notes

This is the core of knowledge and place that absorbs ideas, clippings, to-dos, youtube content, etc. It is for having a structured, bite-sized documentation of things I study and apply.

/portfolio

This is any documentation related to what goes into my career specs like the portfolio itself, CV and Resume.

/projects

This brainstorming documentation for my projects, however it doesn’t store much because all project related documentation goes in the docs/ directory inside the project, code-as-documentation, and in my to-do application.

Other parts of my personal knowledge management are YouTube where most of my knowledge comes from other than blog articles and textbooks; and to manage my schedule, ToDoist.

This will sound something similar to David Allen’s “Getting Things Done” (GTD) Philosophy. Not that I created my own system knowingly, but making a reference to his philosophy does help to clarify what my system is doing. Also kind of a mix of C(apture), O(rganize), D(istill), E(xpress) by Tiago Forte.

Capture: Collect anything and everything that has your attention into an inbox.
Clarify: Determine if captured items are actionable. If not, trash them, incubate them, or file them as reference.
Organize: Sort actionable tasks into logically categorized lists (e.g., next actions, projects, waiting-for).
Reflect: Review and update your lists regularly to maintain clarity and trust in your system.
Engage: Do the work based on your current context, time available, and energy levels.

Let’s go over how we will manage to do each step.

Capture: most of my capture happens within YouTube, blog articles, textbooks, LLM chats.

YouTube -> playlists (watch later, etc.)
Blog articles -> clippings
Textbooks / LLM pinned chats -> inbox


However, this is almost never linear as it seems because in the end, everything passes through an LLM filter for formatting, structuring, and fact checks.

Clarify: from all the data that we have captured from different sources, these will differ in importance and maturity. If the data was a moments thing, which was captured but as an afterthought it’s not something I needed, doesn’t seem as important, or I’m not ready for it yet, it will be deleted/thrown away or it may just stay there as long as it needs and wait its turn to be digested to be part of my notes.
Organize: this I believe is the most important part as it’s what and how knowledge gets absorbed and structured; something like a long term memory. The core would be the /notes directory which absorbs clippings, youtube video informations, completed todo tasks, textbook information, tool documentations, and more. However be aware that everything starts as a small idea and therefore everything starts as a single file and when many related ideas start to clutter the single file it becomes a folder. And this will change a lot over time. Think lots on how to structure your knowledge, as you give more thought the higher the probability of it staying with you longer. The key is malleability, and space to change than it being too rigid as that’s not really how our brain works, which is plastic. Something to note when managing data is also the importance of metadata. That’s why every single folder should have a index.md which is not exactly an index of the ideas inside the folder in the orthodox way but more like an abstract version of what goes in that folder along with the workflow if needed. This is to prevent documentation staleness like what I experienced with the MOC. All files must include some kind of YAML metadata at the top because file names should default to snake casing and no symbols. More of the file naming and project structuring conventions will be provided below.
Reflect: this can happen on purpose, but mostly it should happen unconsciously in my opinion. The reflection should happen along with the engagement. If you have a well organized notes in your own words it should be documentation that you come back to frequently. Then you will realize if things need updates or deletion. And this would happen naturally.
Engage: this is where we apply what we organized in the real world. The default key finding to search for a specific text in a file system in various tools is Command + Shift + F and that’s what works in Obsidian and that’s also what I’ve set on my personal website. This would be a Command + Shift + K in Notion, which I can free from my brain now.

In conclusion, I do know that this system might look a bit too overly complex, but like anything in life it’s only the beginning and it has become natural over time. That’s why this post is also something for myself, as a way to organize my thoughts kind of like a meta cognition. All in all, I would encourage anyone to make their own PKM as there are major benefits to managing a PKM. It reduces cognitive load to remember details; you just have to remember the location, which you put effort to structure so it’s easier to remember. Also, it’s managing an external brain where knowledge compounds over time, adding value.
p.s. From time to time, I think sometimes I’m overengineering stuff, which is bad for productivity. For example, when I spend time restructure the folders and files and how to divide the contents and stuff. However, I think I enjoy doing this and also it makes me understand what I want to document better so do what’s good for you! Good luck!

title: zsh
text:
zsh is a type of shell among many others and the following will be a guide on organizing what goes into each of the zsh configuration files.






Note



There are other components one of which is ~/.zlogin, which will not be covered here because I don’t think it’s as important.

title: zsh
text:
Load Order
This is the whole reason the files differ. zsh reads them in this order:

~/.zshenv  →  /etc/zprofile (path_helper)  →  ~/.zprofile  →  ~/.zshrc  →  ~/.zlogin
   always            login only              login only     interactive

Two consequences do all the work:

~/.zshenv is the only file a non-interactive, non-login shell reads — scripts with a zsh shebang, cron, tools spawning zsh -c.
path_helper runs after ~/.zshenv. It rebuilds PATH from /etc/paths and /etc/paths.d, putting those first, then appends whatever was already set.

title: zsh
text:
.zshenv
Loaded for every zsh invocation. Put plain environment variables here — they survive untouched, because path_helper only rewrites PATH. Reason why you shouldn’t set PATH here as MacOS overrides it.
Because path_helper demotes it, /opt/homebrew/bin set here would lose to /usr/bin, and Apple’s python3 would shadow the Homebrew one.

title: zsh
text:
.zprofile
macOS starts a login shell for each new terminal window, so this runs in practice for every session. It loads after path_helper, so prepends stick.
PATH goes here — Homebrew’s own install instructions say the same:

eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)"   # prepends bin+sbin, sets HOMEBREW_*/MANPATH/INFOPATH
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"

The tradeoff: non-login shells don’t read this, so a zsh script gets the system PATH. If that ever matters, re-prepend inside ~/.zprofile — don’t move PATH to ~/.zshenv.

title: zsh
text:
.zshrc
Interactive-only: aliases, prompt, completions, and tools needing zle (e.g., fzf, zoxide, nvm). It also loads after path_helper, so PATH set here works — but it’s wrong on principle, since a non-interactive login shell would miss it.






Note



An interactive shell reads commands directly from user input (TTY), while a non-interactive shell runs scripts or automated tasks in the backround without user interaction.

Initialization
If you don’t have a project directory run the following command:

uv init <project-title>

If you already have a project directory cd into the directory and run the following command:

uv init

When initializing the project, there are a few files that will be populated: .python-version, hello.py, pyproject.toml, and uv.lock.
Let’s go over what each one does:

.python-version: this is the file used to manage the python version. For example, let’s say that it defaults to python version 3.13 because it’s your global python’s version but you want to use a different version, then you can modify it to 3.12.
hello.py: this is just a basic Python template, so it doesn’t carry much meaning on its own and can safely be deleted.
pyproject.toml: this file is the core of setting up your coding environment. It will be explained further below, but it manages the Python version and can also take on the role of requirements.txt.
uv.lock: there’s no need to touch this file directly.

title: uv
text:
Virtual Environment

Creating the virtual environment
After initializing the project, running the command below will automatically do what python3 -m venv .venv used to do when creating a virtual environment manually:

uv sync

This creates the .venv virtual environment and installs the dependencies by referencing the .python-version, pyproject.toml, and uv.lock files. In fact, you don’t even have to run it explicitly — running any Python script with uv run <script.py> will create the virtual environment the same way if it doesn’t exist yet.


Activating and deactivating






Note



Use uv run for any scripts or packages as uv auto detects your virtual environment.


Normally, every time you come back to a project you would have to activate the virtual environment before running anything:

source .venv/bin/activate

You would then see the terminal prompt change from username project-directory to (.venv) username project-directory, and when you’re done, deactivate it:

deactivate

With uv, none of this is necessary. uv run automatically detects the .venv in your project and runs your script inside it, so you never have to remember to activate the environment every time you return to the project. The commands above are only there in case you want to work inside an activated shell manually.

title: uv
text:
Package Management
This part is where uv truly shines. You no longer have to sit through long download times for large libraries or decipher cryptic error messages from version conflicts like you would with pip or conda.

Adding and removing packages

# Add a package
uv add <package-name==version>

# Remove a package
uv remove <package-name==version>

Occasionally a package name comes with extra options in square brackets. In that case, handle it as follows:

# For example
pip install "fastapi[standard]"

# The uv way
uv add fastapi --extra standard

Think of --extra as replacing the double quotes and square brackets.


Exporting dependencies
Packages are automatically recorded in pyproject.toml along with their versions, but if you’re new to uv and find requirements.txt more comfortable, you can export them by running the following commands in the terminal:

uv pip freeze > requirements.txt

# To install packages from requirements.txt
uv pip install -r requirements.txt

title: Multiple Accounts
text:
Setup gets one GitHub account working on a machine. This page is
for when a machine needs two or more — typically a work account and a personal
one — and every repo has to push as the right one.

title: Multiple Accounts
text:
The one mental model
Git has two identities, and confusing them causes almost every “it pushed as the
wrong user” problem.









Identity
Set by
What it actually does




Commit
user.name / user.email
Stamps a label inside each commit


Auth
your SSH key
Decides which account GitHub thinks you are




GitHub picks the account purely from the SSH key. user.email can say
anything — it will not change which account a push lands under.
Because GitHub refuses to accept the same key on two accounts, each account
needs its own key, and each repo needs a way to say which key to use.

title: Multiple Accounts
text:
Choosing the default
One account keeps plain github.com and every other account gets a host alias.
Make the account you use most often the default. Repos already cloned through
plain github.com keep working, so on an established machine the default is
usually whichever account is already set up — changing it means revisiting every
existing remote.
The choice is per machine. A work laptop and a personal one will often make
opposite calls, and nothing in a repo depends on which way a given machine went.

title: Multiple Accounts
text:
Adding an account
Three steps, once per extra account per machine. Only the differences from
Setup are spelled out here.

1. Generate a key with a distinct filename

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@example.com" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_<alias>

-f is the part that matters. Without it the new key overwrites the default
~/.ssh/id_ed25519. -C is a cosmetic label; the email there has no effect on
authentication.


2. Add the public key to that account
Same as Setup — paste ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_<alias>.pub at
https://github.com/settings/ssh/new.






Warning



Log into GitHub as the account the key belongs to first, and check the
avatar in the top-right before pasting. Adding the key to the wrong account is
the most common failure here, and it fails silently until a push goes astray.




3. Invent a host alias
This is the glue. ~/.ssh/config gets a fake hostname that resolves to the real
GitHub but forces one specific key.

# ~/.ssh/config

Host github.com-<alias>
  HostName github.com                      # connect to the REAL github.com
  User git
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_<alias>   # ...but use THIS key
  IdentitiesOnly yes                       # and only this key
  AddKeysToAgent yes
  UseKeychain yes                          # macOS: remember the passphrase


Host — the alias you type in remote URLs. Any string works;
github.com-<alias> is a readable convention.
HostName — stays real github.com.
IdentitiesOnly yes — required. Without it SSH offers keys in its own
order, hits the default key first, and authenticates as the wrong account.
The default account needs no block of its own, though giving it one with
IdentitiesOnly yes keeps the other keys from leaking into its handshake.

Verify each identity independently — the greeting names the account:

ssh -T git@github.com            # the default account
ssh -T git@github.com-<alias>    # the aliased account

Exit code 1 and “does not provide shell access” is normal. Only the name matters.

title: Multiple Accounts
text:
Per repo
The host in the remote URL is the only thing selecting the account.
OWNER/REPO is identical either way.




Remote URL
Authenticates as




git@github.com:OWNER/REPO.git
the default account


git@github.com-<alias>:OWNER/REPO.git
the aliased account





# clone
git clone git@github.com-<alias>:OWNER/REPO.git

# or repoint an existing remote
git remote set-url origin git@github.com-<alias>:OWNER/REPO.git
git remote -v    # fetch AND push must both show the alias

Auth and authorship are separate, so set the commit identity locally too. Use
--global for the default account only; every aliased account gets a plain
per-repo git config.

git config user.name  "Your Name"
git config user.email "you@example.com"

title: Multiple Accounts
text:
Troubleshooting









Symptom
Cause
Fix




Permission to OWNER/REPO.git denied to <other-user>
Remote uses plain github.com, so the default key answered
git remote set-url origin git@github.com-<alias>:OWNER/REPO.git


Push succeeds but lands under the wrong account
Same cause
git remote -v, then repoint as above


ssh -T greets the wrong name
Public key sits on the wrong account, or IdentitiesOnly yes is missing
Re-add the key to the right account; add the flag


ssh -T asks for a password
IdentityFile path is wrong
ls the path in the Host block


Worked before, wrong again after re-adding a remote
git remote add with the plain URL silently reverts to the default key
Always type the alias




Golden rule: for any non-default account, the remote host is never plain
github.com.
