title: Conventions
text: There is not much to dlt as it’s more like a lightweight tool instead of a framework. That’s why the structure and conventions to setting up dlt is quite free to do as you want. However, there is a .dlt folder, which is a dlt-native way to manage dlt configurations.

title: Conventions
text:
Directory Structure
The directory structure will look like the following:






Note



I manage my dependencies with uv hence the pyprojects.yml, uv.lock, and .python-version files.



dlt_project/
├── .dlt/
│   ├── config.toml                 # non-secret config (log level, runtime, dataset names)
│   ├── secrets.toml                # gitignored — real credentials
│   └── secrets.toml.example        # committed template
│
# >>> custom sources & destinations
├── sources/                        # EXTRACT layer — one package per source
│   ├── __init__.py
│   │
│   ├── {source_a}/
│   │   ├── __init__.py             # @dlt.source + @dlt.resource definitions
│   │   ├── helpers.py              # API client, pagination, auth, retry/backoff
│   │   ├── settings.py             # constants: base URL, endpoints, default params
│   │   └── README.md               # what it pulls, quirks, rate limits
│   │
│   └── {source_b}/
│       ├── __init__.py
│       ├── helpers.py
│       ├── settings.py
│       └── README.md
│
├── destinations/                   # LOAD layer — one package per custom destination
│   ├── __init__.py
│   │
│   ├── {destination_a}/
│   │   ├── __init__.py             # @dlt.destination definitions
│   │   ├── helpers.py              # client, auth, write/flush logic
│   │   └── settings.py             # constants: endpoints, batch size, defaults
│   │
│   └── {destination_b}/
│       ├── __init__.py
│       ├── helpers.py
│       └── settings.py
# <<< custom sources & destinations
│
├── pipelines/                      # LOAD/RUN layer — one runner per pipeline
│   ├── {source_a}_pipeline.py      # dlt.pipeline(...).run({source_a}())
│   └── {source_b}_pipeline.py
│
├── schemas/                        # optional — schema contracts
│   ├── export/                     # dlt writes inferred schemas here
│   └── import/                     # pin/edit schemas here to enforce them
│
├── tests/                          # mirror sources/ structure
│   ├── conftest.py
│   ├── test_{source_a}.py
│   └── test_{source_b}.py
│
├── pyproject.toml                  # deps: dlt[{destination}] + source libs
├── uv.lock
├── .python-version
├── .gitignore                      # ignores .dlt/secrets.toml, .venv, etc.
└── README.md

Below will be an explanation of each of the subdirectories and files in logical order. Meaning that this is the order I would fill in the code to run my pipelines.






Tip



A good way to build a robust pipeline is to think in enhancing the project in the following order: secrets, idempotency, error/retry handling, incremental optimizations, observability, scheduling, tests, schema drifts. This does not apply only for dlt, but for all data pipelines, too.



Why a folder per source
The folder-per-source layout is convention-by-example, not a hard rule — dlt has no docs page mandating it. It is reverse-engineered from dlt’s own built-in sources (dlt/sources/*) and the verified-sources repo. Verified against dlt 1.28.2.









File
Contains
Nature




__init__.py
the @dlt.source function; imports from the others
wiring — reads top-to-bottom as intent


settings.py
static data: BASE_URL, endpoint catalog, defaults, constants
data — no logic


helpers.py
pure functions: resource builders, custom paginators/auth, row transforms
logic — testable in isolation




How dlt’s own shipped sources are laid out:









Source
Files
Notes




filesystem
__init__.py, settings.py, helpers.py, readers.py
The full trio + extra. settings.py is literally DEFAULT_CHUNK_SIZE = 100. readers.py holds format-specific read fns.


sql_database
__init__.py, helpers.py, schema_types.py, arrow_helpers.py
No settings.py — nothing static to hoist. Extra schema_types.py for type mapping.


rest_api
__init__.py, typing.py, config_setup.py, utils.py
It’s a framework, not a source: typing.py = config schema, config_setup.py = config→objects.




So the convention is loose — sources add, skip, and rename files as their needs demand. settings.py only appears when there are shared constants. Add a file when a concern earns one, not to fill a template; an empty helpers.py is fine as a reserved slot.






Note



dlt init scaffolds a single-file *_pipeline.py quickstart, not this folder layout. The folder pattern comes from the verified-sources repo.




Scaling: catalog + builder loop
Past a handful of endpoints, stop hand-writing each resource and go data-driven:









File
Small source
Scaled source




settings.py
flat ENDPOINTS (name→path)
enriched catalog (name→{path, params, write_disposition, primary_key})


helpers.py
(empty)
build_resource(name, spec) + any custom paginator/transform


__init__.py
hand-writes each resource
thin @dlt.source; loops the catalog through the builder




Adding an endpoint then costs one entry in settings.py and zero code change. If __init__.py imports a builder across the module boundary, make it public (build_resource, not _build_resource).

title: Conventions
text:
Configs & Secrets
There are various ways to set up configs and secrets. The one I prefer is to use the .dlt native features. Then use the dlt supported decorators to call them with @dlt.source, @dlt.resource and @dlt.destination.






Note



Environment variables override secrets.toml and config.toml. That’s why if you prefer setting up configs and secrets with environment variables you can do so.



Configs
The configurations are managed by the config.toml. This file is to handle non secret variables.

[runtime]
log_level="INFO"

# Do not compress files sent to the filesystem bucket
[normalize.data_writer]
disable_compression=true

# Recommended sections for the destination (destination.module)
[destination.filesystem]
bucket_url = "s3://[your_bucket_name]"

# Arrow/polars loads skip data-lineage columns by default.
# Turn them on so every row carries 
# _dlt_load_id (joins to _dlt_loads for auditing) and _dlt_id (unique row id).
[normalize.parquet_normalizer]
add_dlt_load_id = true
add_dlt_id = true



Secrets
The secrets are managed by the secrets.toml. This file will have the variables for sources and target. The thing is that there is no hard rules to manage these and the following conventions are “one” of the default ways, but also trying to keep it modular.

[sources.{source_a}]
api_key = "..."

[sources.{source_b}.credentials]
username = "..."
password = "..."

[destination.{destination_a}]
credentials = "db://user:password@service-account/database?warehouse=warehouse_name&role=role"

[destination.{destination_b}.credentials]
host = "..."
username = "..."
password = "..."
database = "..."

If the credentials have a predefined format like SQL database or Object store & filesystem. You can separate by provider name / pipeline name.

[{provider}.sources.filesystem.credentials]
client_email = "..."
private_key = "..."
project_id = "..."

[{provider}.sources.sql_database.credentials]
drivername = "..."
database = "..."
username = "..."
host = "..."
port = "..."

title: Conventions
text:
Pipelines
Normally pipeline files are the starting point. It calls a source and destination through the decorators @dlt.source and @dlt.destination. However, we wouldn’t make all the mess of using dlt for a project that wouldn’t scale. That’s why I plan to start with a scaffold that I’ve provided above in the directory structure part with the tree.
The pipeline script should look something like the following:

import dlt

from sources.{source_dir} import {source_dir}


def run() -> None:
    pipeline = dlt.pipeline(
        pipeline_name="{source_dir}",
        destination="{destination}",
        dataset_name="{source_dir}",
    )
    load_info = pipeline.run({source_dir}())
    return load_info
    

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run()

title: Conventions
Conventions
text:
Variables
Okay, there are a lot of variables to manage, so let’s make a small bullet point list of what values to configure for each of the main variables.

pipeline_name = the domain or source
dataset_name = schema
wrapper = @dlt.source(name={}, section={})
credentials [sources.{source}.filesystem.credentials]

title: Conventions
text:
Environments
To separate environments under .dlt make the following configurations:

.workspace: leave it an empty file, it’s to let dlt create its artifacts in this workspace rather than ~/.dlt.
dev.secrets.toml: exclude variables under secrets.toml that belong to dev and add them here.
prod.secrets.toml: exclude variables under secrets.toml that belong to prod and add them here.
profile-name (Optional): just add a single text no quotations like: dev or prod to pin the runs to a specific profile. However, I’d recommend just using WORKSPACE__PROFILE=prod when running pipelines to prod instead. All runs default to dev.


Put the non-secret half in {profile}.config.toml
A profile overlay works for config.toml too, and that is usually the better
file. dlt resolves a credential field by field across every provider, so a
credential can be split: the part that identifies an environment goes in
committed config, and only the actual secret stays in the gitignored file.

# .dlt/dev.config.toml  -- committed
[destination.postgres.credentials]
database = "dev_maplestory"


# .dlt/secrets.toml  -- gitignored, shared by every profile
[destination.postgres.credentials]
host = "localhost"
port = 5432
username = "..."
password = "..."

The point is reviewability: the environment-to-database map is in git and shows
up in a diff, while nothing secret is. Only fields typed as secrets (password,
API keys) are forced into secrets.toml; everything else resolves from config.


The built-in profiles
dev (the default), prod, tests, and access. dev and tests are
LOCAL_PROFILES — never synced to dltHub. tests is worth wiring even before
there are tests: it exists so a test run cannot touch the data you work
against, and pointing it at a real database rather than a local duckdb file is
what lets it catch destination-specific failures.


State is per profile — this is the real payoff
The workspace moves pipeline state out of ~/.dlt/pipelines/ and into
{run_dir}/.dlt/state/{profile}/pipelines/. Without a workspace, a dev run and
a prod run of the same pipeline_name share one state directory and its
incremental cursors. That, not the config layering, is the reason to reach for
workspaces rather than swapping dataset_name by hand.
Consequence when retrofitting an existing project: the moment .workspace
appears, dlt stops finding the old state. Destination-side state
(_dlt_pipeline_state, _dlt_loads, _dlt_version) lives in the dataset and
is re-synced automatically, so this is usually harmless — but copy
~/.dlt/pipelines/{name} into the new location if the pipeline has incremental
cursors you cannot afford to re-derive.


Gotchas

The marker file is the only trigger: dlt builds a WorkspaceRunContext
if and only if .dlt/.workspace exists. Its contents are never read.
Do not run dlthub init in a directory that already has a .dlt/. It
scaffolds a workspace and overwrites what is there. touch .dlt/.workspace
is the whole retrofit.
dlt --help hides the profile and workspace subcommands until a
workspace is initialized, which makes the feature look absent when it is not.
Commit .workspace and every {profile}.config.toml; gitignore
.dlt/state/, .dlt/data/, .dlt/profile-name, and .dlt/*.secrets.toml.

Checking what a profile resolves to, without running a load:

WORKSPACE__PROFILE=tests python -c "
from dlt.common.configuration.resolve import resolve_configuration
from dlt.destinations.impl.postgres.configuration import PostgresCredentials
print(resolve_configuration(PostgresCredentials(), sections=('destination','postgres')).database)
"



Name the environment in the database, not the dataset
If the destination is Postgres, put the environment in the database
(dev_maplestory, prod_maplestory) and keep dataset_name identical across
profiles. Prefixing the dataset instead means every downstream source
definition and query carries the environment as a string.
One naming trap: dlt derives its staging dataset from
staging_dataset_name_layout, default %s_staging. A dataset named nexon
produces a schema nexon_staging, which collides in meaning with a dbt
staging layer in the same database. Prefix raw datasets — raw_nexon gives
raw_nexon_staging, which reads unambiguously.

title: Conventions
text:
Scripts
when running:
- WORKSPACE__PROFILE=prod # default: dev
- INGESTION__{key}={value} # e.g., INGESTION__MONTHS_BACK={int|all} (default: 3)
- PROGRESS=log
- PIPELINES__{pipeline_name}__REFRESH={drop_sources|drop_resources|drop_data}

title: REST APIs
text:
dlt gives you two ways to pull a REST API. Default to the low-level one.
The declarative rest_api source reads nicely in a demo and fights you the moment the API misbehaves. Real APIs misbehave: they return HTTP 200 with an error envelope, echo params back in a different type than you sent, need a delay between calls, or need one field re-stamped after the response lands. Every one of those is two lines in a resource body and a config-schema hunt in the declarative version. See Scaling: catalog + builder loop — an endpoint catalog plus a builder function gets you the same one-line-per-endpoint economy without giving up Python.

title: REST APIs
text:
Auth is not parameters
Two different things, easy to conflate:

Auth — shared by every request, so it lives on the client once.
Query params (ocid, date, world_name, …) — per-request, so they live in the resource that makes the call.


client = RESTClient(
    base_url=BASE_URL,
    auth=APIKeyAuth(name="x-api-key", api_key=api_key, location="header"),
)

A new query param never touches auth.

text:
Appendix — declarative rest_api config
Kept for the times you read someone else’s config, or an API is boring enough to deserve one.

Source of truth: <venv>/lib/python*/site-packages/dlt/sources/rest_api/typing.py. The TypedDicts there always win over this page. Written against dlt 1.28.2.


config = {
    "client": {...},              # required
    "resources": [...],           # required
    "resource_defaults": {...},   # merged into every resource — use for shared hints
}

client: base_url (req), headers, auth, paginator (default "auto"), session.
resources[] — a bare string ("posts", name==path==table) or a dict: name, endpoint, include_from_parent, max_table_nesting, selected, parallelized, processing_steps, plus any dlt.resource hint (write_disposition, primary_key, merge_key, columns, table_name, schema_contract, parent).
endpoint: path (supports {resources.<name>.<field>} templating), method, params, json, data, paginator, data_selector (JSONPath), response_actions, incremental, auth, headers.
auth — pick with type:








type
Keys




bearer
token


api_key
name, api_key, location (header|query|cookie)


http_basic
username, password


oauth2_client_credentials
access_token_url, client_id, client_secret, access_token_request_data, default_token_expiration




paginator — auto (default) · single_page · json_link (next_url_path) · header_link (links_next_key) · header_cursor (cursor_key, cursor_param) · cursor (cursor_path, cursor_param, has_more_path) · offset (limit, offset_param, limit_param, total_path, maximum_offset, stop_after_empty_page) · page_number (page_param, base_page, total_path, maximum_page, stop_after_empty_page, has_more_path).
incremental: cursor_path, start_param, end_param, initial_value, convert (+ all standard IncrementalArgs).
processing_steps — in-flight transforms: filter (row) -> bool, map (row) -> row, yield_map (row) -> Iterator[row].
Fan-out, declaratively — the equivalent of the transformer chain above is a resolve param plus a data_selector on the parent:

{
    "name": "character_list",
    "endpoint": {
        "path": CHARACTER_LIST,
        # resolve reads a TOP-LEVEL field of each record the parent yields,
        # so the parent must yield character-level records for `ocid` to be visible.
        "data_selector": "account_list[*].character_list[*]",
    },
},
{
    "name": "character_basic",
    "endpoint": {
        "path": CHARACTER_BASIC,
        "params": {"ocid": {"type": "resolve", "resource": "character_list", "field": "ocid"}},
    },
},

The tension the transformer chain avoids: that data_selector also changes what character_list stores — character rows instead of the raw account payload. You cannot keep the raw payload and fan out from the same resource.

Naming
text:
Meta Names
_{layer}__{sources|models}.yml
The main characteristic of meta yaml files is that the naming starts with an underscore.

{layer}_{domain}__{entity}_{temp}_{version}.sql










Slot
Required
Rule




{layer}
yes
stg, int, dim, fct, bridge


{domain}
yes

{entity}
yes

{temp}
no

{version}
no

title: Layers
text:
We follow Kimball’s three layered data warehouse: staging, intermediate, marts. The medallion names for the same three are bronze, silver, gold. The modeling theory behind this sits in the Data Modeling section — this page is only about how the layers land in dbt.
Each layer gets its own page. Read the matrix first, then the page for the layer you are writing in.

title: Layers
text:
Where the Line Is
The layer descriptions can read as confusing because staging also transforms. The difference is business logic. Staging casts, renames, and normalizes so the data is usable, and keeps every single detail and data from the raw source while doing it. The moment a transformation encodes a business decision, it belongs in intermediate.
Contracts sit on the two boundaries that other people depend on: staging, because everything downstream reads it, and marts, because the business reads it. Intermediate is ours to churn, so it carries no contract. The contract format is in Documentation.

title: Materializations & Build Time
text:
The Ladder
You would start with a view (which the build time would be fast), move to table (which the query time would be fast), and later to incremental materializations (which the build time is moderate and the query time would be fast).










Materialization
Build time
Query time
Use when




view
fast
slow
staging, and intermediate until it hurts


table
slow
fast
marts, heavy intermediate models


incremental
moderate
fast
the full rebuild stops being worth it




Defaults per layer are set in dbt_project.yml, see Project Structure. Per-model overrides go in the model itself with a config() block, see Styling.

title: Materializations & Build Time
text:
Incremental Models
Only use merge, it’s the only idempotent closes to “set-it-and-forget-it”.
Remember to add the logic to erase orphaned data.
If the data is too big for merge, then use delete+insert or insert_overwrite.
delete+insert checks for a set of keys that you define.

title: Materializations & Build Time
text:
Prune Early
The cheapest optimization is not scanning the data in the first place. In an import CTE, select only the columns the model actually uses and push the where filter as high as it goes, so every join and transformation below it works on a smaller set.

with

orders as (

    select
        order_id,
        customer_id,
        order_total,
        order_date

    from {{ ref('orders') }}

    where order_date >= '2020-01-01'

)

Staging is the exception. A select * off a { source() } is allowed there, because the layer exists to carry every raw column forward — see Staging. Everywhere else, an import CTE that selects * is leaving build time on the table.

title: Materializations & Build Time
text:
Project-wide Optimizations
The project-wide optimizations would require something like dbt State if you’re willing to go for a freemium or premium subscription.
For the free way to do this would be to chain selectors like state:modified, source_status:fresher, config.materialized:view. Selector syntax is in Node Selection.

title: Documentation
text:
The documentation that you can manage with dbt is vast. The goal is to make documentation for components of data governance: Data Catalog & Glossary, Data Contracts & Schema Registries, Data Lineage, Security & Acess Control Policies.



Business Glossary: Define standard business terms (e.g., what exactly constitutes an “Active User”?).

semantic layer

Data Dictionary: Map columns, data types, and descriptions for every core table or collection.

_model.yml






Data Contract: Open Data Contract Standard (ODCS)

dbt model contracts
Fundamentals: Every data contract starts with its fundamentals: the version of the standard, unique identifier, name, data contract version number, and status. This metadata identifies the contract and enables versioning.
Schema: The schema defines the structure and semantics of your data. Here we define the table structure with its columns. Each property includes technical details, business semantics, and governance attributes.
Data Quality: Data quality rules ensure that data meets expectations. Define checks like valid value constraints, row count thresholds, and custom SQL validation logic. These can be tested automatically with the Data Contract CLI.
Team: Document who owns and maintains the data contract. Include team name, description, and members with their roles. Add support channels, how data consumers can reach out to the owners.
Terms of Use: Define the purpose, usage guidelines, and limitations for your data. This helps consumers understand what they can and cannot do with the data, establishing clear governance boundaries.
SLAs: Service Level Agreements define non-functional guarantees. Data consumers can match these with their use-case requirements.
Servers: Finally, specify where the data lives. The server configuration includes connection details for different environments.



# Fundamentals
apiVersion: v3.1.0
kind: DataContract
id: orders
name: Orders
version: 1.0.0
status: active

# Terms of Use
description:
  purpose: "Provides order and line item data for analytics and reporting"
  usage: "Used by analytics team for sales analysis and business intelligence"
  limitations: "Contains only the last 2 years of data"
  customProperties:
    - property: "sensitivity"
      value: "secret"
      description: "Data contains personally identifiable information"
  authoritativeDefinitions:
    - url: "https://entropy-data.com/policies/gdpr-compliance"
      type: "businessDefinition"
      description: "GDPR compliance policy for handling customer data"

# Schema & Quality
schema:
  - name: orders
    physicalType: TABLE
    description: All historic web shop orders since 2020-01-01. Includes successful and cancelled orders.
    properties:
      - name: order_id
        logicalType: string
        description: The internal order id for every orders. Do not show this to a customer.
        businessName: Internal Order ID
        physicalType: UUID
        examples:
          - 99e8bb10-3785-4634-9664-8dc79eb69d43
        primaryKey: true
        classification: internal
        required: true
        unique: true
      - name: customer_id
        logicalType: string
        description: A reference to the customer number
        businessName: Customer Number
        physicalType: TEXT
        examples:
          - c123456789
        required: true
        unique: false
        logicalTypeOptions:
          minLength: 10
          maxLength: 10
        tags:
          - pii:true
        classification: internal
        criticalDataElement: true
      - name: order_total
        logicalType: integer
        description: The order total amount in cents, including tax, after discounts.
          Includes shipping costs.
        physicalType: INTEGER
        examples:
          - "9999"
        quality:
          - type: text
            description: The order_total equals the sum of all related line items.
        required: true
        businessName: Order Amount
      - name: order_timestamp
        logicalType: timestamp
        description: The time including timezone when the order payment was successfully
          confirmed.
        physicalType: TIMESTAMPTZ
        businessName: Order Date
        examples:
          - "2025-03-01 14:30:00+01"
      - name: order_status
        businessName: Status
        description: The business status of the order
        logicalType: string
        physicalType: TEXT
        examples:
          - shipped
        quality:
          - type: library
            description: Ensure that there are no other status values.
            metric: invalidValues
            arguments:
              validValues:
                - pending
                - paid
                - processing
                - shipped
                - delivered
                - cancelled
                - refunded
            mustBe: 0
    quality:
      - type: library
        metric: rowCount
        mustBeGreaterThan: 100000
        description: If there are less than 100k rows, something is wrong.
  - name: line_items
    physicalType: table
    description: Details for each item in an order
    properties:
      - name: line_item_id
        logicalType: string
        description: Unique identifier for the line item
        physicalType: UUID
        examples:
          - 12c9ba21-0c44-4e29-ba72-b8fd01c1be30
        logicalTypeOptions:
          format: uuid
        required: true
        primaryKey: true
      - name: sku
        logicalType: string
        businessName: Stock Keeping Unit
        description: Identifier for the purchased product
        physicalType: TEXT
        examples:
          - 111222333
        required: true
      - name: price
        logicalType: integer
        description: Price in cents for this line item including tax
        physicalType: INTEGER
        examples:
          - 9999
        required: true
      - name: order_id
        required: false
        primaryKey: false
        logicalType: string
        physicalType: UUID
        relationships:
          - type: foreignKey
            to: orders.order_id
            
# Servers
servers:
  - server: production
    environment: prod
    type: postgres
    host: aws-1-eu-central-2.pooler.supabase.com
    port: 6543
    database: postgres
    schema: dp_orders_v1
    
# Team
team:
  name: sales
  description: This data product is owned by the "Sales" team
  members:
    - username: john@example.com
      name: John Doe
      role: Owner
  authoritativeDefinitions:
    - type: slack
      url: https://slack.example.com/teams/sales
roles:
  - role: analyst_us
    description: Read access for analytics to US orders
  - role: analyst_eu
    description: Read access for analytics to EU orders
    
# SLAs
slaProperties:
  - property: availability
    value: 99.9%
    description: Data platform uptime guarantee
  - property: retention
    value: "1"
    unit: year
    description: Data will be deleted after 1 year
  - property: freshness
    value: "24"
    unit: hours
#    element: orders.order_timestamp # enable this to check freshness with Data Contract CLI
    description: Within 24 hours of order placement
  - property: support
    value: business hours
    description: Support only during business hours
price:
  priceAmount: 0
  priceCurrency: USD
  priceUnit: monthly
tags:
  - e-commerce
  - transactions
  - pii
customProperties:
  - property: dataPlatformRole
    value: role_orders_v1
contractCreatedTs: "2025-01-15T10:00:00Z"

title: Node Selection
text:
The selection language that decides which nodes a command touches. The commands themselves are in Workflow.
“Node” and “resource” mean the same thing here: models, tests, sources, seeds, snapshots, exposures, analyses — everything in the DAG.

title: Node Selection
text:
Which Commands Take Selection








Command
Arguments




run, test, build
--select, --exclude, --defer


seed, snapshot, source freshness, docs generate
--select, --exclude


ls, build
--select, --exclude, --resource-type


compile
--select, --exclude, --inline

title: Node Selection
text:
Always Quote the Argument

dbt build --select "tag:nightly"

Unquoted selectors are unreliable across shells and terminals — *, +, and spaces all get mangled. Quote every time, single argument or not.

title: Node Selection
text:
How Selection Resolves
dbt applies the pieces in a fixed order, then filters by resource type:

Methods (tag:, path:, …) match a set of nodes.
Graph operators (+, @) expand each set along the DAG.
Set operators (space, comma) combine the expanded sets.
--exclude subtracts.
Anything that is not the current task’s resource type is dropped — only models survive dbt run, only seeds survive dbt seed.

Step 5 is why dbt run --select "tag:nightly" silently skips the nightly-tagged seeds. Use dbt build when the selection spans resource types.

title: Node Selection
text:
Methods
method:value. The method is omittable — it defaults to path, file, or fqn — but write it out; an implicit method is a selector nobody can read.









Method
Selects
Example




tag:
nodes carrying a tag
"tag:nightly"


path:
nodes at or under a directory or file
"path:models/staging/github"


file:
a model by filename, with extension
"file:stg_issues.sql"


fqn:
nodes by fully-qualified name — the dbt ls output format
"fqn:my_project.staging.stg_issues"


package:
nodes from a package; package:this for the root project
"package:dbt_utils"


config.<key>:
nodes with a matching config
"config.materialized:incremental"


resource_type:
nodes of one type
"resource_type:source"


source:
models downstream of a source, with +
"source:snowplow+"


exposure:
parents of an exposure, with +
"+exposure:weekly_kpis"


test_type:
unit, data, generic, singular
"test_type:singular"


test_name:
instances of one generic test
"test_name:unique"


state:
nodes changed against a comparison manifest
"state:modified+"


result:
nodes by their status in the prior run
"result:error"


source_status:
sources refreshed since the last freshness check
"source_status:fresher+"


group:, access:, version:
governance properties
"access:public"




config. reaches into nested values too — config.meta.contains_pii:true, config.grants.select:reporter, config.unique_key:column_a against a list.
Unix wildcards work in most methods: * any run of characters, ? one character, [abc] and [a-z] one from the set.

dbt ls --select "package:*_source"
dbt ls --select "*.marts.*"

title: Node Selection
text:
Graph Operators

dbt run --select "+my_model"    # my_model and every ancestor (upstream)
dbt run --select "my_model+"    # my_model and every descendant (downstream)
dbt run --select "+my_model+"   # both directions

Quantify the + to stop at a given depth:

dbt run --select "my_model+1"    # first-degree children only
dbt run --select "2+my_model"    # parents and grandparents
dbt run --select "3+my_model+4"  # 3 up, 4 down

The @ operator goes in front only. It selects the model, all its descendants, and the ancestors of those descendants — everything needed to actually build the downstream set in an environment where the parents may not exist yet. This is the CI operator.

dbt build --select "@my_model"

title: Node Selection
text:
Set Operators
The whitespace-versus-comma distinction is the one that bites.









Separator
Meaning
Example




space
union — matches any argument
"+stg_orders +stg_customers"


comma, no space
intersection — matches every argument
"marts.finance,tag:nightly"





# everything upstream of either model
dbt run --select "+snowplow_sessions +fct_orders"

# only the shared ancestors of both
dbt run --select "+snowplow_sessions,+fct_orders"

# mixed: two intersections, unioned by the space between them
dbt run --select "+snowplow_sessions,+fct_orders marts.finance,tag:nightly"

Argument order inside an intersection is irrelevant. A node matched twice appears once.

title: Node Selection
text:
Exclude
--exclude takes the same syntax as --select and subtracts its result.

dbt run --select "my_package.*+" --exclude "my_package.a_big_model+"
dbt test --exclude "test_name:relationships"

title: Node Selection
text:
Preview Before Running
dbt ls resolves a selector and prints the nodes without executing anything. Use it whenever a selector is more than one term — it is the difference between a wrong CI job and a five-second check.

dbt ls --select "state:modified+" --state prod-artifacts/
dbt ls --select "source_status:fresher+"

title: Node Selection
text:
Indirect Test Selection
Selecting a model pulls in its tests too. How aggressively is the --indirect-selection flag:








Mode
Behaviour




eager (default)
include every test touching a selected node


cautious
skip tests that also have unselected parents


buildable
like cautious, but keep the test if a selected node is an ancestor


empty
only tests attached solely to the selected node




eager is right in development. In CI, where half the DAG is deferred to production, cautious or buildable stops a relationships test from running across two environments at once.

title: Node Selection
text:
Named Selectors
Once a selector stops fitting on one line, move it to a top-level selectors.yml and give it a name.

selectors:
  - name: nightly_diet_snowplow
    description: Non-incremental Snowplow models that power nightly exports
    definition:
      union:
        - intersection:
            - '@source:snowplow'
            - 'tag:nightly'
        - 'models/export'
        - exclude:
            - intersection:
                - 'package:snowplow'
                - 'config.materialized:incremental'

union: and intersection: are the keyword forms of the space and comma operators. A definition can also be a bare CLI-style string ('tag:nightly', operators and all) or a method: value pair, which supports no operators at all.
Invoke it with the --selector flag:

dbt run --selector nightly_diet_snowplow

A selector marked default: true applies to any command run without --select or --exclude. Only one may be default per invocation.






--selector does not combine, on v1.11



Passing --selector alongside --select or --exclude makes dbt use --selector and silently ignore the others. The selector: method — --select "selector:my_selector tag:nightly" — that fixes this is v1.12 and later. On v1.11, one or the other.

title: Node Selection
text:
State Comparison
state: compares the project against a manifest from a previous run, supplied by --state or DBT_ENGINE_STATE. This is what makes a CI job build only what a pull request changed.








Selector
Matches




state:new
no node with this unique_id in the comparison manifest


state:modified
every new node, plus every changed one


state:old
the node exists in the comparison manifest


state:unmodified
existing and unchanged




state:modified has subselectors when the full criteria are too broad:








Subselector
Detects




.body
model SQL, seed values


.configs
any node config except database / schema / alias / tags / meta


.relation
database / schema / alias — the warehouse representation


.persisted_descriptions
description changes, only where persist_docs is on


.macros
upstream macro changes, direct or indirect


.contract
a model contract’s column name or data_type




tags and meta are metadata-only: changing either never triggers state:modified, because neither affects materialization. description does count, but only with persist_docs enabled.






Do not point --state at target/



dbt overwrites target/manifest.json during parsing, before it reads it for comparison — so the comparison finds nothing, and the error reads as “saved manifest not found”. Copy the production manifest into a separate directory (prod-artifacts/, state/) and point --state there. Never let --state and --target-path be the same path.

title: Node Selection
text:
Defer
--defer resolves ref() calls against the --state manifest instead of the current target, for any node that is both unselected and absent from the database. It lets a handful of end-of-pipeline models build against production parents instead of rebuilding the DAG in a dev schema.

dbt build --select "state:modified+" --defer --state prod-artifacts/

Both --defer and --state are required. --favor-state goes further: prefer the state manifest even when the node does exist in the target. Ephemeral models are never deferred — they are pass-throughs for other ref calls.
--defer-state takes a second manifest, so state:modified can compare against one point in time while deferral falls back to another. Unset, it reuses --state, which is what you want almost always.






Deferred runs cross environments



A deferred run reads dev data and production data in the same query. A relationships test between a selected model and a deferred parent is comparing across environments — and a dev-only row limit that production does not have will quietly change the result.

title: Node Selection
text:
Reusing the Last Run
result: reads the prior invocation’s artifacts, so a failed build can be resumed instead of restarted.

dbt run   --select "result:error" --state target/        # rerun what errored
dbt build --select "1+result:fail" --state target/       # rebuild models behind failed tests
dbt build --select "1+result:fail+" --state target/      # and everything downstream of them

result:fail is test-only. result:error matches any resource that errored. Tests have no descendants, so result:fail+ on its own returns nothing but the test — the 1+ prefix is what reaches the model.
Pair it with source freshness to run only what new data touched:

dbt source freshness
dbt build --select "source_status:fresher+" --state prod-artifacts/

title: Setup
text:
Locate Binaries

ls /usr/lib/postgresql

Add the binary path permanently to your shell config file.

echo 'export PATH="/usr/lib/postgresql/{version}/bin:$PATH"' >> ~/.zshrc
source ~/.zshrc

Verify the tools are active.

which initdb pg_ctl psql

title: Setup
text:
Initialize Database
Create a directory inside your home folder to hold and own the database files and initialize with your user as a superuser.

initdb -D $HOME/pgdata -U $USER -A trust

title: Setup
text:
Configure the Port & Socket (Optional)
By default, PostgreSQL tries to bind to port 5432 and write sockets to system directories requiring sudo. You can update configuration to use the port of your liking and Unix socket folder /tmp.

# Change port
sed -i 's/#port = 5432/port = {port}/' $HOME/pgdata/postgresql.conf

# Set socket directory to /tmp
sed -i "s|^#*unix_socket_directories = .*|unix_socket_directories = '/tmp'|" $HOME/pgdata/postgresql.conf

# Direct psql to the /tmp
echo 'export PGHOST=/tmp' >> ~/.bashrc
source ~/.bashrc

title: Setup
text:
Start the Server
Start the server process in the background (-D) using pg_ctl and direct logs to a dedicated file.

pg_ctl -D $HOME/pgdata -l $HOME/pgdata/server.log start

Check it’s working.

# Verify status of server
pg_ctl -D $HOME/pgdata status

# Check live logs
tail -f $HOME/pgdata/server.log

title: Setup
text:
Connect to the Server

psql -p 5432 -d postgres

title: Installation
text: There are two ways to put GA4 on a site, they look almost identical, and the difference matters.

title: Installation
Installation
section: Google Tag Manager — a container, not a tag
text:
Google Tag Manager — a container, not a tag
GTM measures nothing on its own. It is a container you fill with tags through a web console, plus the delivery mechanism that fetches and fires them. Its entire value is changing what you track without touching code or redeploying.

<script>(function(w,d,s,l,i){ /* loads gtm.js?id=GTM-XXXXXXX */ })(window,document,'script','dataLayer','GTM-XXXXXXX');</script>

If you never open the console and configure tags, a GTM container does exactly nothing — while still downloading its runtime on every pageview.

title: Installation
section: Loading both is the classic double-count
text:
Loading both is the classic double-count
Because GTM is a box that can hold a copy of the thing, this happens easily:

page loads
├── gtag.js       → page_view → G-XXXXXXXXXX
└── GTM container → GA4 tag   → page_view → G-XXXXXXXXXX   ← same property, second hit

Two hits, one visitor. Every figure in the reports doubles — for every visitor, not just you — and nothing in the GA4 interface flags it. The usual path in is chronological rather than careless: GA4 hands you the gtag.js snippet when you create a data stream, and GTM’s own setup wizard later walks you into creating a GA4 Configuration tag. Neither step mentions the other.
Pick one. Hardcoded gtag.js is simpler and one less request; GTM earns its keep only once you actually want to add or change tags without a deploy. If both are already present, audit the container before assuming which to remove.

title: Installation
Auditing a Container
text:
A GTM container’s published configuration is served publicly at its own URL. You do not need console access, or even to own the container, to see exactly which tags it fires. This is the fastest way to answer “what is this thing actually doing” — on your own site or anyone else’s.
The response is the GTM runtime with the container’s configuration embedded in it as a JSON blob under a "resource" key.

title: Auditing a Container
text:
Quick answers by grep
Usually enough on its own — find out which analytics properties a container reports to:

grep -oE '"(G-[A-Z0-9]{6,}|UA-[0-9]+-[0-9]+|AW-[0-9]+|DC-[0-9]+)"' gtm.js | sort -u

If a measurement ID you already load directly via gtag.js shows up here too, you have a double-count.

title: Auditing a Container
text:
Reading the tag list properly
Brace-match the "resource" object out of the file and parse it:

import json

s = open('gtm.js', encoding='utf-8', errors='replace').read()
start = s.index('{', s.find('"resource":'))
depth, j, instr, esc = 0, start, False, False
while j < len(s):
    c = s[j]
    if instr:
        if esc: esc = False
        elif c == '\\': esc = True
        elif c == '"': instr = False
    else:
        if c == '"': instr = True
        elif c == '{': depth += 1
        elif c == '}':
            depth -= 1
            if depth == 0: break
    j += 1

r = json.loads(s[start:j+1])
print('version:', r.get('version'))
for k in ('tags', 'macros', 'predicates', 'rules'):
    print(f'{k:12}', len(r.get(k) or []))

Reading the result:

tags — what actually fires. An empty list means the container does nothing at all.
predicates / rules — the trigger conditions. Zero of these alongside zero tags confirms an untouched container.
macros — variables. A handful ship with every container, so a small count here is not evidence of configuration.
version: 1 with nothing else is the signature of a container that was created and never published into.

Tag entries carry a function field identifying the type: gaawc is a GA4 Configuration, gaawe a GA4 Event, html a custom HTML tag, img a tracking pixel.

title: Auditing a Container
section: An empty container is not free
text:
An empty container is not free
The finding worth acting on is usually not a misconfiguration but dead weight. An empty container still downloads its runtime on every single pageview — on the order of 100 KB gzipped — to execute nothing. Measure it rather than guessing:

curl -s -H "Accept-Encoding: gzip" -o /dev/null \
     -w "%{size_download} bytes\n" \
     "https://www.googletagmanager.com/gtm.js?id=GTM-XXXXXXX"

Delete the snippet if the container is empty. GTM’s value is changing tags without a redeploy, which an empty container is not providing, and the snippet pastes back from the console the moment you actually want it.

title: Porting from pandas
text:
The dangerous differences between pandas and polars are not the ones that raise.
.empty → .is_empty() and .tolist() → .to_list() fail loudly the first
time the code runs. The four below return a number, just a different one, and
only show up if you diff against the old implementation on real data.
Port with a harness: run both implementations over the same real frame and the
same input combinations, and compare cell by cell. Every item on this page was
found that way, not by reading the diff.

title: Porting from pandas
section: group_by keeps null keys; groupby drops them
text:
group_by keeps null keys; groupby drops them
pandas groupby silently drops rows whose key is NaN. Polars gives null its own
group. A key that is null in even a fraction of a percent of rows can aggregate
into a group large enough to outrank real ones — and it renders as an unlabelled
axis tick or pie slice.

# pandas: rows with a null key simply vanish
df.groupby("category")["revenue"].sum()

# polars: same result requires saying so
df.drop_nulls("category").group_by("category").agg(pl.col("revenue").sum())

pivot(index=...) has the same asymmetry — pivot_table drops null index rows,
pivot keeps them. Audit every grouping key for nulls before assuming parity;
df.null_count() is the fast way to find which keys can actually be null.

title: Porting from pandas
section: Neither sort is stable, so ties are undefined in both
text:
Neither sort is stable, so ties are undefined in both
polars sort is unstable by default. But pandas sort_values defaults to
kind="quicksort", which is also unstable — so the pandas output being diffed
against had an arbitrary tie order to begin with. Do not chase an exact match on
tied rows; make the new code deterministic instead.

pivot = (
    df.pivot(on="period", index="key", values="revenue", aggregate_function="sum")
    .fill_null(0)
    .sort("key")                                        # seed a defined order
    .sort(latest_period, descending=True, maintain_order=True)  # stable from there
)

Two things matter, and one alone is not enough: maintain_order=True makes the
sort stable, and the seed sort decides what stability preserves. pandas got its
seed for free because pivot_table returns a sorted index; pivot returns
first-seen order. With both, tied rows break by key in both libraries and the
frames match exactly — including anything derived from row position, such as a
rank-change arrow, which otherwise drifts by ±1 wherever a tie moved.

title: Porting from pandas
section: Null propagates through is_in and comparisons
text:
Null propagates through is_in and comparisons
pl.col(x).is_in(values) yields null for a null x, not False. This is
invisible on the positive branch and wrong on the negative one: filter(~expr)
drops those rows from both sides, so a row present in the pandas output
disappears from the polars one and the two branches no longer sum to the total.

matched = pl.col("key").is_in(wanted).fill_null(False)
hit  = df.filter(matched)["revenue"].sum()
miss = df.filter(~matched)["revenue"].sum()   # needs the fill_null to balance

Same for str.contains, which is where pandas spells it na=False.

title: Porting from pandas
section: Plotly reads order from the data, so sort instead of category_orders
text:
Plotly reads order from the data, so sort instead of category_orders
pd.Categorical plus category_orders forced legend and axis order regardless
of row order. Dropping both means the explicit sort is the ordering — plotly
takes trace and category order from first appearance. An explicit sort is also
faster than making either pandas or plotly do it.
Sort by the series key first when one series spans every x value:

rank = {name: i for i, name in enumerate(SERIES_ORDER)}
df = (
    df.with_columns(_order=pl.col("series").replace_strict(rank, default=len(rank)))
    .sort(["_order", "x"])   # leading series covers every x, so the axis stays complete
    .drop("_order")
)

Sorting by x first instead would take legend order from whichever series happens
to appear at the earliest x. Sorting by series first is only safe when the
leading series is present at every x — a total or “all” series usually is. For a
stacked bar where no category is guaranteed complete, sort ["x", category]
instead, so the axis comes out right and the stack order falls out of the
category’s own collation.

title: Porting from pandas
section: Lazy is where the memory actually goes
text:
Lazy is where the memory actually goes
.lazy() on an already-loaded frame does not shrink the frame — it defers the
work. What it buys is that a filter/aggregate chain never materialises the
intermediates, and projection pushdown means only the columns the chain really
reads get built. On a wide fact table sliced to a small window, that is the
difference between a full-width copy per interaction and a few hundred rows.

base = df.lazy().filter(...)              # nothing has run yet
cur  = base.filter(date_between).group_by(key).agg(...).collect()

Two things to keep straight:

Collect once where a result is reused. Separate .collect() calls on the
same LazyFrame redo the work; the engine caches nothing between them. If three
views share a filtered base, collect it once and pass the DataFrame.
Do not mix eager and lazy in one chain. A join between a DataFrame and a
LazyFrame raises, and a .collect() on an eager frame raises
AttributeError: 'DataFrame' object has no attribute 'collect'. Convert at the
top of the section and stay in one mode.

Scalars are worth taking off a LazyFrame too: a min/max for an axis bound is
lf.select(pl.col(c).min()).collect().item(), not a materialised column.

title: Porting from pandas
text:
Things with no polars equivalent

pd.Period — use a monotonic month index (year * 12 + month - 1) for
arithmetic, and inclusive date bounds for filtering. pd.DateOffset(months=i)
becomes a subtraction on that index.
pd.Categorical ordering — a numeric sort-key column plus an explicit sort.
.mode() — polars’ is unordered where pandas’ is sorted, so
.mode().sort().first() is what matches .mode().iloc[0].
A pandas Styler — no equivalent, and Streamlit’s conditional table
colouring is Styler-only. Convert with .to_pandas() at that boundary and
keep everything above it polars; the frame being styled is a display-sized
aggregate, not source data. Watch the dtype: with_row_index gives UInt32,
and appending a NaN summary row collapses an unsigned column to object,
which breaks a "{:.0f}" format. Cast to float64 first.

title: Porting from pandas
text:
A few more that bite

cut() returns an Enum, not a String. Joining that against a String key
raises SchemaError: datatypes of join keys don't match. Cast it.
A local variable named pl silently shadows the polars import for the rest
of its scope. Grep for it before starting a port.
pandas 2.3 PeriodDtype has no .freqstr. Code doing
getattr(dtype, "freqstr", "") to branch on frequency has been taking the
fallback branch since that attribute moved — worth checking rather than
porting the bug forward.

title: Porting from pandas
section: Parsing and dtype at the boundary
text:
Parsing and dtype at the boundary

Decimal columns — a SQL NUMBER arrives as pl.Decimal, and
.to_pandas() turns it into an object column of decimal.Decimal that raises
TypeError on division by a float. Cast at the read boundary, not at the use
site, so no downstream page has to know.
"YYYY-MM" text — chrono needs a day component, so str.to_date("%Y-%m")
will not parse it. Concatenate "-01" first and use %Y-%m-%d with
strict=False for the pandas errors="coerce" behaviour.

title: Streamlit
text:
Multi-pages
There are two generations, and they do not coexist quietly.

v1 (2022) — convention based. Files in a pages/ directory next to the entrypoint become the sidebar automatically. No code, and no way to filter the list.
v2 (1.36+) — st.Page + st.navigation. You declare the pages, so you can filter them by role. This is the one to use.


Never name the directory pages/
If a directory called pages sits next to the entrypoint, Streamlit decides the app is v1 — and it decides before your entrypoint runs:

# streamlit/runtime/scriptrunner/script_runner.py
if PagesManager.uses_pages_directory:   # True iff <entrypoint dir>/pages exists
    _mpa_v1(self._main_script_path)     # globs pages/*.py, runs the REQUESTED page
else:
    exec(code, module.__dict__)         # your entrypoint

uses_pages_directory is a class attribute computed once per process (runtime/pages_manager.py) and only cleared by st.navigation — which your entrypoint never reaches on that first run. So on the first script run of a fresh process, a deep link runs pages/<name>.py instead of the entrypoint.
Everything the entrypoint does is skipped: auth gates, monkey-patches, the nav itself. If access control lives only in which pages you pass to st.navigation, that is an auth bypass on any cold process — and containers give you a cold process on every deploy.
It self-heals once any run reaches st.navigation, which makes it maddening to reproduce. Two things hide it:

A reload is not enough. The flag is per process — you must restart the server.
The URL must be a deep link. Hitting / runs the entrypoint (it is the default page) and looks completely normal.

Reproduce it in 20 seconds: drop a pages/probe.py that writes a marker, cold-start, open /probe. The marker renders with no login.
Fixes, in order of preference:

Name the directory something else — dashboards/, views/. _mpa_v1 hardcodes the string "pages" in exactly two places, so any other name makes the legacy path unreachable. One rename, done.
Move the entrypoint so <entrypoint dir>/pages does not exist (entrypoint at repo root, pages under the package).
Keep pages/ but put every page one level down in subdirectories — _mpa_v1 globs pages/*.py non-recursively, so nesting keeps it empty. This is what a real production app I read does.

Whatever you pick, also gate each page itself. A nav filter is not an access check — nothing stops a page being reached another way. One guard helper — login, domain, and per-page role check — as the first statement of every page, and a test that asserts every page calls it with its own filename.
client.showSidebarNavigation = false does not help. Despite what the config docstring says, commands/navigation.py applies it to any sidebar position, so it hides your real v2 nav too.

title: Streamlit
section: st.stop() is not an early return
text:
st.stop() is not an early return
Every tab in a multi-tab page is rendered on every script run — the tab widget
only chooses what is visible. So a guard that bails out of one tab with
st.stop() halts the whole run and leaves every later tab blank.
There is no early return out of a with tab: block either, since it is not a
function. The guard has to be an if/else around the tab body:

with tab:
    ...prepare data...
    if frame.is_empty():
        st.info("...")
    else:
        ...the rest of the tab...

Verify with git diff -w — if the only real change is the guard, the rest of
the diff is the re-indentation and reads as noise.

title: Streamlit
text:
Filters & Components

This package is something that I will build myself as a side project, but that I could use at work too as I develop dashboards solo for now. I might merge my dashboards with the IT team at some point (I’m in the Big Data Team) though.






Note



This is no right or wrong when it comes to UI/UX and the following components that I use for the filters is a convention for myself, but it would be a good place to start. Without a convention or system to structure your filters, a dashboard can become messy real quick.
#### Swapping Data (Radio)


When swapping data use a radio. By this it means when you have to change the criteria. For example, making a big change in how your data is queried like switching the date column. Imagine that normally you display your data in date_utc, but then you have Korean users and make it date_kst. That’s swapping the column that was part of the grain. Also, if this is a filter that you would like to put at the top of the dashboard like a global filter, or in a side by for a vertical stack

Choosing from an Enum (Segmented Control)
Use a segmented control when you want to toggle between views like timeframes or metrics. This is a horizontal layout so keep that in mind. Also, this works clean with short texts or emojis.

Optimizations
@st.cache_data
@st.cache_resource
@st.fragment (parallel=True)
st.form
st.session_state + st.empty()

Do not copy a cached frame into session_state
A pattern that looks like caching and is actually the opposite:

@st.cache_data
def load(): ...

if "data" not in st.session_state:          # DON'T
    st.session_state.data = load()
df = st.session_state.data.copy()

st.cache_data is already a cache, and it is global (scope="global" by default): one copy shared by everyone. session_state is per session, so this makes a private full copy of the frame for every logged-in person, on top of the shared one. With a 3 GB frame and four people, that is 12 GB of duplicates.
It also breaks refresh. st.cache_data.clear() cannot touch anyone else’s session_state, and session_state has no TTL — so other users stay pinned to old data indefinitely, with nothing on screen saying so.
Just call the cached function. cache_data returns a fresh copy per call, so mutation safety is unchanged:

df = load()



A refresh button is global, and silent for everyone else
st.cache_data.clear() wipes the cache for all users, not just the presser. But Streamlit never pushes to a session — other people see new data on their next interaction, not immediately. Worth knowing before you promise “refresh updates everyone”.
Clear cache_resource too if a database connection is cached there; the same button then doubles as auth-token recovery. Do not clear session_state — that throws away the user’s filters.

title: Performance
text:
A dashboard that takes 30 seconds to load does not get used. People go back to asking for a raw extract and doing it in a spreadsheet. Performance is a UI/UX concern, not an infrastructure one.
The mental model: every dashboard has a cost at three layers — the query, the transport, and the render. Fixing the wrong layer wastes effort, so find out which one is slow before optimizing.

title: Performance
text:
Minimize fields and records
The cheapest data is the data you never fetch. Push filtering as far upstream as possible — into the query, not into the dashboard after the data has already arrived. Same for columns: select only what the view actually uses. Pulling every column drags unused data across the wire and into memory.
Defaults matter here. If a date filter defaults to “all time”, every user pays for a full scan on first load. Default to a narrow recent window and let people widen it deliberately.

title: Performance
section: Reduce the marks in the view
text:
Reduce the marks in the view
A “mark” is one data point drawn on screen — a bar, a dot, a cell. Rendering cost scales with mark count, and past a few thousand marks the client is the bottleneck, not the data source.

Load top N and let the user drill for the rest.
Paginate tables. Nobody scrolls 50,000 rows.
Watch the cardinality of whatever is on the axes. A bar chart grouped by a unique ID is not a chart, it is a table with extra steps. Group by a dimension with tens of values, not thousands.
Aggregate before plotting. If the chart shows a monthly trend, aggregate to month upstream instead of sending daily rows and rolling them up in the view.

The cardinality point is the one people miss. Filtering rows helps, but if the grouping dimension is high-cardinality the mark count stays high regardless.

title: Performance
text:
Prefer cheap types
Comparisons on integers and booleans are much cheaper than on strings, and they compress better in columnar storage.

Continuous date filters (a range: from x to y) over discrete lists of date strings. A range is a scan boundary; a list of strings is N equality checks and usually defeats partition pruning.
Booleans over status strings when the flag is genuinely binary.
Integer keys for joins and filters, with the label joined on only for display.

The general rule: filter on the number, display the string.

title: Performance
text:
Materialize your tables
Views are fine for development and for thin logic on top of an already-small table. In a real company the data is not small, and a dashboard built on a stack of views re-executes that whole stack on every interaction — every filter change, every page load, every user.
Materialize the table that backs the dashboard. Let the dashboard hit one pre-aggregated table, and move the joins and window functions into a scheduled build. The dashboard query should be close to reading one table with a date filter.
This trades freshness for speed, which is almost always the right trade for BI — stakeholders making weekly decisions do not need second-level freshness. Ask what refresh interval the decision actually requires before assuming real-time.

title: Performance
text:
Cache
Once the query is as small as it will get, cache the result so repeated views do not re-run it. Whatever the tool’s caching mechanism is, match its expiry to the upstream refresh schedule — expiring sooner than the data changes only buys re-queries for identical results.

text:
Data Mart Core Architecture
To build a scalable analytical layer, your fact tables should mirror the natural state transitions of an entity (e.g., an order or a batch of product) as it moves through the supply chain.
The data should be prepared using a Conformed Dimension Data Mart approach. This means that your fact tables directly around the 6 execution phases are wrapped tightly by an Orchestration (Log/Audit) dimension to track pipeline health and end-to-end latency.

1. Orchestration & Lineage (The Dimension/Audit Layer)
Before analyzing the business, you must analyze the pipeline. This layer tracks data quality, ingestion latencies, and end-to-end processing times.

Core Dimension/Fact: dim_pipeline_execution, fact_data_lineage
Key Columns: dag_run_id, source_system_status, ingestion_timestamp, transformation_latency_seconds, data_quality_score
Dashboard Visual: Data pipeline health monitoring, source-to-target latency gauges, rows processed per hour.



2. Plan (The Forecasting Mart)

Core Fact Table: fact_demand_forecast
Grain: One row per Product_ID per Location_ID per Forecast_Period_Month.
Key Columns: forecast_quantity, historical_actual_quantity, capacity_limit_units, safety_stock_threshold
Dashboard Visual: Forecast Accuracy KPI (MAPE), Actual vs. Forecasted Demand trends, Capacity Utilization charts.



3. Order (The Digital Transaction Mart)

Core Fact Table: fact_order_lifecycle
Grain: One row per Order_Line_Item.
Key Columns: order_id, customer_id, order_status_code (Created, Approved, Invoiced), order_placement_timestamp, gross_amount, tax_amount, discount_amount
Dashboard Visual: Daily/Monthly Revenue, Total Orders Placed, Order conversion rates, Average Order Value (AOV).



4. Source (The Procurement Mart)

Core Fact Table: fact_purchase_orders
Grain: One row per Purchase_Order_Line_Item.
Key Columns: po_number, supplier_id, po_creation_timestamp, expected_delivery_date, actual_received_date, ordered_quantity, received_quantity, unit_cost
Dashboard Visual: Supplier Lead Time, Supplier OTIF (On-Time In-Full), Procurement spend analysis by vendor.



5. Transform (The Manufacturing & Quality Mart)

Core Fact Table: fact_production_runs
Grain: One row per Production_Batch_ID or Work_Order_ID.
Key Columns: work_order_id, product_id, production_start_timestamp, production_end_timestamp, total_units_produced, defective_units_count, machine_downtime_minutes
Dashboard Visual: First Pass Yield (FPY %), OEE (Overall Equipment Effectiveness), Defect Rate by product line, Production Downtime trends.



6. Fulfill (The Logistics & Distribution Mart)

Core Fact Table: fact_shipment_fulfillment
Grain: One row per Shipment_ID / Waybill.
Key Columns: shipment_id, order_id, warehouse_id, carrier_id, allocated_timestamp, shipped_timestamp, delivered_timestamp, promised_delivery_date, shipping_cost
Dashboard Visual: Perfect Order Index (POI), Shipping/Last-Mile Cost per order, Warehouse processing time (Click-to-Ship latency).



7. Return (The Reverse Logistics Mart)

Core Fact Table: fact_order_returns
Grain: One row per Return_Line_Item.
Key Columns: return_id, original_order_id, return_request_timestamp, return_reason_code, disposition_status (Restocked, Refurbished, Scrapped), refund_amount
Dashboard Visual: Return Rate % by product category, Top Reasons for Returns, Financial impact of refunds vs. scrap loss.



Conformed Dimensions (The “Glue”)
To build an executive dashboard that allows filtering the entire supply chain by a specific product, location, or date, these dimension tables must link seamlessly across all 6 fact tables above:

dim_products — product_id, SKU, category, brand, cost_price, retail_price
dim_locations — location_id, site_name, type (Warehouse, Plant, Store), region, country
dim_date — date_id, calendar_date, day_of_week, month, quarter, year, fiscal_period



Executive Dashboard Layout Strategy
When setting up your BI tool (Tableau, Power BI, Looker, etc.), structure it into three distinct operational layers:

The Executive Summary (High Level): Place 4–5 global KPIs at the very top: Total Revenue (Order), Global OTIF % (Fulfill), Forecast Accuracy (Plan), and Gross Margin %.
The Supply Chain Funnel (Process Flow): Build a chronological funnel visualization or linear timeline tracking an order’s lifecycle. Show the average duration (in hours/days) it takes to pass through each phase: Order Placed → PO Raised → Produced → Shipped → Delivered.
The Operational Drill-Downs (Tabbed Views): Create dedicated tabs for specific team playbooks (e.g., a “Procurement Tab” powered by the Source Mart, a “Plant Operations Tab” powered by the Transform Mart).

Metrics






Info



Three overarching focus areas, spread across 8 performance attributes.








Warning



These are not all the metrics. These top metric are the level 1 metrics, but they can funnel down until level 3 metrics (so start with top metrics and dive as you get mature).



1. Resilience Focus (Customer-Facing)

Reliability (RL): Measures process predictability and execution quality.

Top Metric: Perfect Order Fulfillment (RL.1.1)

Responsiveness (RS): Measures operational execution speed and cycle times.

Top Metric: Order Fulfillment Cycle Time (RS.1.1)

Agility (AG): Measures system adaptability and capacity to handle unexpected external shifts or disruptions.

2. Economic Focus (Internal Business)

Costs (CO): Measures total operational expenditures incurred across the pipeline.

Top Metric: Total Supply Chain Management Costs (CO.1.1)

Profit (PR): Measures the direct bottom-line financial outcome generated by the supply chain.

Top Metric: Earnings Before Interest and Taxes (EBIT) as a Percent of Revenue (PR.1.1)

Asset Management Efficiency (AM): Measures capital utilization and asset turn speeds.

Top Metric: Cash-to-Cash Cycle Time (AM.1.1)




3. Sustainability Focus (Outward Impact)

Environmental (EV): Measures resource footprints, waste generation, and green performance.

Top Metric: Materials Used / Total Footprint (EV.1.1)

Social (SC): Measures corporate responsibility, labor compliance, and governance safety protocols.

Top Metric: Diversity and Inclusion / Policy Compliance Score (SC.1.1)

text:
TL;DR: Yes, the core execution platforms (ERP, WMS, TMS, MES) form the operational backbones, but a modern enterprise supply chain relies on several upstream, downstream, and analytical systems to bridge design, planning, procurement, and customer interaction.
Here is the structured breakdown of the primary execution platforms alongside the additional essential systems in the supply chain ecosystem.

🏛️ Complete Supply Chain Architecture Map
Below is how these systems fit together from a data engineering perspective:

🧩 Other Key Systems in the Ecosystem
Beyond execution platforms, supply chain pipelines frequently ingest from and sync to these specialized layers:

PLM (Product Lifecycle Management): Tracks a product from design concept to engineering sign-off. It passes the Bill of Materials (eBOM to mBOM) downstream to the ERP and MES to dictate what parts to buy and manufacture.
SRM (Supplier Relationship Management): Manages upstream vendor interactions before a purchase order is committed to the ERP. Data pipelines ingest SRM data to assess vendor risk and lead-time variability.
OMS / CRM (Order Management & Customer Relationship): Captures customer orders and feed them into the ERP or WMS for fulfillment.
SCP / S&OP (Supply Chain Planning / Sales & Operations Planning): Acts as the “brain” sitting on top of the ERP. It runs optimization algorithms to forecast demand and calculate safety stock levels.



🔄 The Broader Pipeline Synchronization Challenge
Similar to the ERP vs. WMS inventory valuation disconnect, data engineers must manage several cross-system synchronization patterns:

PLM ↔︎ ERP Sync: Ensures engineering design changes (e.g., swapping a component) update the ERP’s purchasing records before orders are placed.
OMS ↔︎ WMS Sync: Handles real-time allocation to ensure an item shown as “in stock” on an e-commerce platform is actually available in the physical warehouse.
ERP ↔︎ Planning System (SCP): Requires low-latency streaming of real-time sales and stock burn-rates to automatically recalculate procurement schedules.

TL;DR: The ERP is the only 100% strictly necessary system—it is the non-negotiable financial engine and single source of truth. Everything else is modular and scale-dependent: micro-businesses can run entirely on an ERP (or even basic spreadsheets), adding specialized execution, design, or planning systems only as physical and operational complexity demands it.


System Hierarchy: Core vs. Supplementary
Here is how the systems break down by operational necessity:










Tier
Systems
Why It Fits This Tier
Can You Start Without It?




Tier 1: Non-Negotiable Core
ERP
Manages the general ledger, purchasing, invoicing, and tax compliance. Without this, you cannot legally operate or report financials.
No. (Even a small business needs at least a lightweight ERP or accounting database like QuickBooks/Xero).


Tier 2: Operational Execution (Needed once physical scale increases)
WMS TMS MES
Manages complex spatial storage, transportation routing, and factory floor machines.
Yes. Small/mid-sized operations handle these directly inside the ERP using basic inventory receipts, manual shipping tags, and simple work orders.


Tier 3: Specialized & Upstream (Needed for specific business models)
PLM SRM OMS / CRM
Manages CAD design changes, complex vendor negotiations, and multi-channel customer pipelines.
Yes. Standard products don’t need PLM, simple purchasing doesn’t need SRM, and B2B models often bypass dedicated CRM/OMS tools.


Tier 4: Analytical Layer (Needed at enterprise scale)
SCP / S&OP
Runs predictive algorithms, machine learning forecasts, and safety stock simulations.
Yes. Companies routinely run planning on basic historical trends or external data warehouses/BI tools.






How Companies Scale Into the Stack

Phase 1 (Startup / Small Business): You only run an ERP. Physical stock tracking, simple shipping, and basic reorder points live inside basic ERP tables.
Phase 2 (Growth / Production): If you open a factory, you add an MES. If you open a large distribution center, you add a WMS to optimize aisle picking because the ERP’s basic inventory view isn’t fast or granular enough.
Phase 3 (Enterprise Scale): As freight costs surge, you add a TMS. As product lines expand, you add PLM and SCP to automate supply and demand forecasting.

title: HTTP to HTTPS
text:
HTTPS is not a different protocol. It is the same HTTP request and response, wrapped in a TLS tunnel before it leaves the machine. Two things happen inside that wrap:

Encryption — nobody between the browser and the server can read or modify the bytes.
Identity — the server proves it really is example.com by presenting a certificate signed by a Certificate Authority (CA) the browser already trusts.

The encryption is the easy part; any process can generate a key pair in a second. The identity part is the whole problem. A certificate is a CA’s signed statement that “whoever holds this private key controls this domain name”. You cannot manufacture that yourself — you have to prove domain control to a CA, and the CA hands back a certificate that expires (Let’s Encrypt: 90 days).
So “turn on HTTPS” really means three separate jobs:

Get a domain name that resolves to your public IP.
Prove to a CA that you control it, and receive a certificate.
Terminate TLS on port 443 with that certificate, and keep renewing it forever.

title: HTTP to HTTPS
section: What You Need Before Anything Works
text:
What You Need Before Anything Works









Requirement
Why
How to check




A real domain name
Certificates are issued for names, never for bare IPs. https://203.0.113.5 cannot be made valid.
dig +short app.example.com


DNS A/AAAA record pointing at your public IP
The CA connects back to that name to verify you.
dig +short app.example.com matches curl -s ifconfig.me


Ports 80 and 443 reachable from the internet
Port 80 is used for the ACME HTTP-01 challenge and for the HTTP→HTTPS redirect. 443 serves the real traffic.
curl -I http://app.example.com from outside your network


Router port-forward / cloud firewall rule
Home servers need 80 and 443 forwarded to the host; cloud VMs need the security group opened.
Same as above










Warning



Many residential ISPs block inbound port 80 and 443, and CGNAT means you may not own your public IP at all. If curl from outside times out, no amount of Docker configuration will fix it — see No Public Port 80 below.

title: HTTP to HTTPS
section: Why You Do Not Add TLS to the App Container
text:
Why You Do Not Add TLS to the App Container
The instinct is to make the application itself speak HTTPS. Almost always wrong:

Every app then needs its own certificate logic, its own renewal cron, and its own copy of the private key.
Renewal usually needs a restart, so the app goes down every 60 days.
Only one container can bind port 443. A second service means a second host or a second port.
Application servers (gunicorn, uvicorn, the Streamlit dev server, node) are not hardened for direct internet exposure.

The standard pattern instead: the app keeps speaking plain HTTP, and a reverse proxy in front of it terminates TLS.

internet --443/TLS--> [ reverse proxy ] --80/plain HTTP--> [ app container ]
                       (owns the cert)     (docker network, never published)

This is safe because the plain-HTTP leg never leaves the Docker bridge network. Traffic between containers on the same user-defined network does not touch the host’s NIC or the internet.
The key Docker consequence: stop publishing the app’s port. Use expose (or nothing at all — containers on the same network reach each other by service name regardless) instead of ports. If you leave ports: - "8000:8000" in place, anyone can bypass your proxy and hit the app over plain HTTP.

services:
  app:
    image: myapp:latest
    expose:
      - "8000"        # visible to other containers only
    # ports:          # <- delete this; it publishes to the host
    #   - "8000:8000"

title: HTTP to HTTPS
text:
The Lazy Default: Caddy
Caddy gets a certificate from Let’s Encrypt on first boot, redirects HTTP to HTTPS, and renews in the background, with no cron job and no extra container. For a new setup this is the shortest path that is also correct.
Caddyfile:

app.example.com {
    reverse_proxy app:8000
}

docker-compose.yml:

services:
  app:
    image: myapp:latest
    expose:
      - "8000"

  caddy:
    image: caddy:2-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "80:80"
      - "443:443"
    volumes:
      - ./Caddyfile:/etc/caddy/Caddyfile:ro
      - caddy_data:/data      # certificates live here — must persist
      - caddy_config:/config
    depends_on:
      - app

volumes:
  caddy_data:
  caddy_config:

docker compose up -d, then https://app.example.com works. That is the whole setup.
Two details that matter:

caddy_data must be a named volume. Certificates and the ACME account key are stored there. Lose it and every docker compose up requests fresh certificates, which walks straight into Let’s Encrypt’s rate limit (5 duplicate certificates per week).
The upstream is app:8000, not localhost:8000. Inside a container, localhost is that container itself. Docker’s embedded DNS resolves the Compose service name.

Multiple services are one block each:

app.example.com {
    reverse_proxy app:8000
}

dashboard.example.com {
    reverse_proxy streamlit:8501
}

title: HTTP to HTTPS
HTTP to HTTPS
text:
Traefik
Worth it when containers come and go and you do not want to edit proxy config for each one. Traefik reads the Docker socket and configures itself from labels on each service.

services:
  traefik:
    image: traefik:v3
    restart: unless-stopped
    command:
      - --providers.docker=true
      - --providers.docker.exposedbydefault=false
      - --entrypoints.web.address=:80
      - --entrypoints.web.http.redirections.entrypoint.to=websecure
      - --entrypoints.web.http.redirections.entrypoint.scheme=https

      - --certificatesresolvers.le.acme.email=you@example.com
      - --certificatesresolvers.le.acme.storage=/letsencrypt/acme.json
