Warning



Mounting /var/run/docker.sock gives that container root-equivalent control of the host. Mount it read-only, and do not do it on a box where the proxy is also running untrusted workloads.

title: HTTP to HTTPS
HTTP to HTTPS
text:
Local Development
For localhost and LAN work there is no CA that will issue you a certificate. Two options:

mkcert — creates a local CA, installs it into the OS and browser trust stores, and issues certificates for any name. No warnings, no public DNS.

mkcert -install
mkcert app.localhost localhost 127.0.0.1
# mount app.localhost+2.pem and app.localhost+2-key.pem into the proxy

Caddy’s internal CA — tls internal in a site block issues a self-signed certificate automatically. Zero setup, but browsers warn until you trust Caddy’s root manually.

app.localhost {
  tls internal
  reverse_proxy app:8000
}


Never reuse a development certificate in production, and never disable certificate verification in clients to work around a warning — that removes the identity guarantee that is the entire point.

title: HTTP to HTTPS
section: Making the App Behave Behind a Proxy
text:
Making the App Behave Behind a Proxy
Once TLS terminates at the proxy, the app receives plain HTTP and — unless told otherwise — thinks the request was insecure. Symptoms: redirect loops, http:// links in generated pages, login cookies rejected, every client IP logged as the proxy’s.
The proxy must send the forwarding headers (Caddy and Traefik do it by default; nginx needs the proxy_set_header lines above), and the app must be configured to trust them:








Framework
Setting




Django
SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER = ("HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PROTO", "https"), plus the public hostname in ALLOWED_HOSTS and CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS


FastAPI / uvicorn
--proxy-headers --forwarded-allow-ips="*"


Flask
werkzeug.middleware.proxy_fix.ProxyFix(app.wsgi_app, x_proto=1, x_for=1)


Streamlit
--server.headless true; proxy must forward websocket upgrade headers or the page loads and then hangs on “Connecting…”


Express
app.set("trust proxy", 1)










Warning



Only trust forwarding headers when a proxy you control is actually in front. A directly-exposed app that trusts X-Forwarded-For lets any client spoof its own IP past rate limits and IP allowlists.

title: HTTP to HTTPS
text:
Checklist and Gotchas

Delete ports: from every app service. Anything still published bypasses TLS.
Persist the certificate volume (caddy_data, /etc/letsencrypt, acme.json). Otherwise every rebuild re-issues and hits Let’s Encrypt’s rate limit — 5 duplicate certificates per exact name set per week.
Test against the staging CA first. Let’s Encrypt staging issues untrusted certificates but has generous limits: Caddy acme_ca https://acme-staging-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory, certbot --staging. Switch to production only after the flow works end to end, and delete the staging certificates when you do.
Point DNS before the first start. Requesting a certificate for a name that does not yet resolve to you burns a failed-validation attempt.
acme.json needs mode 600 if bind-mounted; Traefik refuses to start otherwise. A named volume avoids the issue.
Add HSTS only when HTTPS is stable. Strict-Transport-Security tells browsers to refuse plain HTTP for that domain for the stated duration, and it is cached client-side — you cannot take it back by removing the header. Start with a short max-age, and leave includeSubDomains/preload alone until certain.
Renewal is the part that breaks. It fails months later, silently, usually because port 80 got closed or the webroot mount changed. Check expiry from outside: echo | openssl s_client -connect app.example.com:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates.

title: Visual Studio Code
text:
Precedence is workspace → folder → user. A .code-workspace carries its own
"settings" block, and it silently wins over user settings — including a stale
absolute path that no longer exists. When a setting refuses to take effect, read
the .code-workspace first.



VS Code resolves it, but only in workspace settings. In user settings it
is passed through literally (Could not resolve interpreter path '${workspaceFolder}/...'). python.defaultInterpreterPath is one of these.
The extension resolves it in its own code, in which case it works in user
settings too — ruff.path for example.

Nothing in the UI distinguishes them. Grep the bundle:

grep -o 'workspaceFolder[^"]\{0,60\}' ~/.vscode/extensions/<ext>/dist/*.js | sort -u

Its own value.replace("${workspaceFolder}", ...) means it works anywhere.



${workspaceFolder} becomes folders[0] — the first entry in the
.code-workspace, not the folder owning the file. Extensions often compound it
by querying the workspace rather than the folder:

api.settings.getExecutionDetails(workspace.workspaceFile)  // workspace-scoped

Symptom: opening the folder directly works, opening it inside the multi-root
workspace fails. That asymmetry means per-folder .vscode/settings.json is
never consulted, so the fix is one shared tool env pinned in the
.code-workspace:

uv venv ~/.venvs/<tool>
uv pip install --python ~/.venvs/<tool>/bin/python <tool>==<version>

Pin to the newest project in the window, and prefer this over borrowing a member
repo’s .venv, which breaks when that repo is rebuilt.

title: Format and Dialect
text:
Markdown dialect
Quarto reads Pandoc’s markdown, and from: selects which extensions are enabled. The value is a Pandoc format spec: a base name followed by +/- extension toggles.

format:
  html:
    from: markdown+autolink_bare_uris+hard_line_breaks

Two extensions worth knowing because they change how ordinary prose renders:








Extension
Effect




autolink_bare_uris
a bare https://… becomes a link without <> or []()


hard_line_breaks
a single newline renders as <br> instead of being folded into the paragraph




hard_line_breaks matches how Obsidian and most note apps behave. It also means source files must not be soft-wrapped: a paragraph broken across several source lines will render with visible line breaks at each one.
The full extension list is in the Pandoc manual.

title: Navigation
text:
A website project reads a website: block for site-level chrome.
page-navigation adds previous/next links at the foot of each page, ordered by the sidebar. llms-txt: true emits an llms.txt index plus a plain-markdown .llms.md alongside each page.

title: Navigation
text:
Navbar

website:
  navbar:
    title: "Displayed name"
    background: light
    search: true
    left:
      - icon: github
        href: https://github.com/org/repo
    right:
      - href: index.md
        text: Home
      - href: notes/index.md
        text: Notes

Items go in left, center, or right. Each is text + href, icon + href, or a menu of nested items. An href pointing at a source file is rewritten to the rendered URL.

title: Navigation
text:
Sidebars
A site can define several sidebars. Each gets an id, and Quarto shows the one whose contents include the current page:

website:
  sidebar:
    - id: notes
      title: "Notes"
      collapse-level: 1
      tools:
        - icon: arrow-left-circle
          text: Back
          href: notes/index.md
      contents:
        - text: "Overview"
          href: notes/index.md
        - notes/topic/001-first.md
        - auto: "notes/other-topic/"









Key
Effect




id
identifies the sidebar; a page appearing in its contents selects it


contents
entries: a bare path, a text/href pair, a section with nested contents, or auto


collapse-level
depth at which sections start collapsed


tools
icon links pinned above the contents


style
floating or docked




auto: takes a glob or directory and generates entries from what is on disk, ordered by filename. A directory’s index.md becomes the section landing page, and each entry’s label comes from that file’s title frontmatter, not its filename. Numbering filenames is the usual way to control order, since sorting is lexicographic — zero-pad so 010 does not sort before 002.
Mixing explicit entries and auto: in one contents list is allowed, which is what makes a generated sidebar possible while keeping a hand-written entry at the top.

The sidebar drives more than the sidebar
Two page features are derived from it, which makes turning a sidebar off more destructive than it looks:

page-navigation walks the sidebar order. Prev/next is not chronological or filesystem order — it is the flattened sidebar contents. Set sidebar: false on a page and its prev/next links disappear entirely; list the same page twice under different sections and paging through the site visits it twice.
Breadcrumbs are the sidebar ancestry, and a section’s crumb is its section: string verbatim. There is no per-item badge, so anything decorative added to a section title — a count, an emoji — shows up in the breadcrumb above the page’s <h1> too.

page-navigation: false also works per page, which is how a listing page opts out: the listing is the page, so there is nothing sensible to page to, and Quarto would otherwise emit a lone unstyled link to whichever entry sorts first.

title: Lua Filters
text:
A Lua filter is a script that rewrites the document’s abstract syntax tree between parsing and writing. It is the supported way to add syntax Pandoc does not know, or to transform elements site-wide.
Listed at project level they run on every document, in list order. A document can add its own with a filters key in frontmatter.

title: Lua Filters
text:
Writing one
Define a function named after an AST element type. It receives the element and returns a replacement, a list of elements, or nil to leave it untouched.

-- Wrap every table so it can scroll on narrow screens.
function Table(tbl)
  return pandoc.Div(
    { tbl },
    pandoc.Attr("", { "table-responsive" })
  )
end

Common entry points: Str, Code, CodeBlock, BlockQuote, Table, Div, Header, Link, Image. A Pandoc(doc) function receives the whole document and runs last, which is where document-wide work belongs.
pandoc.Attr(identifier, classes, attributes) builds the attribute triple every element constructor takes. Constructors mirror the element names: pandoc.Div, pandoc.Para, pandoc.Plain, pandoc.Str, pandoc.RawBlock("html", "…").
To reparse a string as markdown rather than emitting it literally:

local blocks = pandoc.read(text, "markdown").blocks

title: Lua Filters
text:
Ordering
Filters see the AST as the previous filter left it. A filter that creates new elements must run before any filter expected to process what it created — a filter that turns a fenced block into nested content has to precede the one that styles code blocks, or the nested code is never visited.

title: Lua Filters
text:
Quarto specifics
quarto.doc.input_file holds the path of the file being rendered, which is the reliable way to scope a filter to a subtree:

function Pandoc(doc)
  local input = quarto.doc.input_file or ""
  if not input:find("/posts/") then return nil end
  -- …
end

Two behaviours that are easy to get wrong:

Quarto’s own filters run on the initial AST. Elements a user filter creates afterwards are never seen by them. Emitting a Quarto construct — a callout, a tabset — by producing the div that Quarto’s filter would have produced does not work; the markup that filter generates has to be emitted directly.
Some frontmatter keys never reach doc.meta. Quarto lifts certain keys into template variables before user filters run, so a filter gating on one of them reads an empty value. body-classes is one — set it in a _metadata.yml to scope CSS to a folder and it still reads as empty from Lua. Gate on the input path instead.

Quarto’s Lua API is documented at quarto.org/docs/extensions/lua-api; the Pandoc module is documented at pandoc.org/lua-filters.

title: Publishing
text:
GitHub Pages
quarto publish gh-pages renders and pushes the result to a gh-pages branch. The branch is machine-generated and should never be edited by hand.
In CI, the same thing is done with the official actions:

- uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/setup@v2

- uses: quarto-dev/quarto-actions/publish@v2
  with:
    target: gh-pages
  env:
    GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

The job needs permissions: contents: write to push the branch. setup@v2 accepts a version input to pin Quarto; without it the latest release is installed, so a render that passes locally can fail in CI on a version difference.
Other target values are netlify, posit-connect, confluence, and quarto-pub.

title: Publishing
text:
Deploying only when something changed
Because render is the expensive step, a scheduled workflow can compare the current inputs against what is already deployed and skip the render when they match — fetch the deployed copy of the generated file, diff it against a freshly generated one, and gate the remaining steps on the result. This keeps a daily refresh job cheap when most runs are no-ops.

title: Setup
text:
What is Flashing and Why
An .iso is not a normal file you copy — it is a byte-for-byte image of a whole disk, including its partition table and bootloader. Flashing means writing those bytes to the USB stick starting at sector 0, so the stick becomes a clone of that disk.
Why a plain copy fails:

Firmware does not read your filesystem. At power-on, the UEFI firmware looks for an EFI System Partition and a boot file at a fixed location (/EFI/BOOT/BOOTX64.EFI). Drag-and-dropping ubuntu.iso onto the stick puts one large file inside the stick’s existing filesystem. The boot structures stay buried inside it, so firmware finds nothing bootable.
The image brings its own partition table. Ubuntu ships a hybrid ISO that boots on both legacy BIOS and UEFI. That dual layout lives in the first sectors of the image — outside any file — so it can only arrive by raw write.
Raw writes are destructive and privileged. Flashing overwrites the partition table, so the stick’s old contents are gone, and the OS requires admin rights to write a block device directly. That is why every tool below asks for a password and shows a scary confirmation.

The same logic applies to .img.xz images for ARM boards; those are pre-installed system images rather than installers, so the flashed card is the finished system.






Warning



Flashing writes to whatever device you select. Selecting your own laptop’s disk destroys it, and there is no undo. Confirm the device by size and name before every write.

title: Setup
text:
Pick a Flashing Tool




Tool
Version
Platform
Use it when

4.15
Windows
Default on Windows. Fastest, handles ISO quirks, portable single .exe.

2.1.6

You want one simple GUI everywhere: pick image, pick drive, flash.


Raspberry Pi Imager
2.0.10
Windows / macOS / Linux
Flashing SD cards or ARM .img.xz images. 2.0 adds a setup wizard that pre-seeds cloud-init (hostname, user, SSH key, Wi-Fi) before first boot.

You install OSes often. Installed once to the stick, then you just copy .iso files onto it and choose at boot — no reflashing per image.

Any of them produce the same bootable stick. Rufus for Windows, dd or Etcher for macOS, Pi Imager for cards.

title: Setup
text:
Download and Verify the Image
Grab the server image for your architecture:

x86: ubuntu-26.04-live-server-amd64.iso (~2.7 GiB) — the installer image.
ARM boards / SBC: ubuntu-26.04-preinstalled-server-arm64+raspi.img.xz from cdimage — no installer, boots straight into a running system.


cd ~/Downloads
curl -O https://releases.ubuntu.com/26.04/ubuntu-26.04-live-server-amd64.iso
curl -O https://releases.ubuntu.com/26.04/SHA256SUMS
curl -O https://releases.ubuntu.com/26.04/SHA256SUMS.gpg


Step 1: Check the Checksum
A truncated or corrupted download produces an installer that fails halfway, usually with a confusing error. Comparing hashes takes ten seconds.

# macOS
shasum -a 256 --ignore-missing -c SHA256SUMS

# Linux
sha256sum --ignore-missing -c SHA256SUMS

Expected output:

ubuntu-26.04-live-server-amd64.iso: OK



Step 2: Check the Signature (Optional but Cheap)
The checksum only proves the file matches SHA256SUMS. Verifying the GPG signature proves SHA256SUMS itself came from Canonical, which matters when you download from a random mirror.

gpg --keyid-format long --keyserver hkp://keyserver.ubuntu.com \
  --recv-keys 0x46181433FBB75451 0xD94AA3F0EFE21092
gpg --keyid-format long --verify SHA256SUMS.gpg SHA256SUMS

Look for Good signature from "Ubuntu CD Image Automatic Signing Key" with fingerprint 8439 38DF 228D 22F7 B374 2BC0 D94A A3F0 EFE2 1092.






Note



gpg: WARNING: This key is not certified with a trusted signature! is expected — you never signed Canonical’s key personally. The fingerprint matching is the check that counts.

title: Setup
text:
Flash the Stick

Rufus (Windows)

Insert the USB stick and run rufus-4.15.exe.
Device: select the stick — verify by capacity, not by drive letter.
Boot selection: SELECT and choose the ISO.
Partition scheme: GPT, Target system: UEFI (non CSM). Use MBR + BIOS or UEFI only for pre-2012 hardware.
START. If asked about downloading Syslinux/GRUB files, allow it.
Wait for READY, then CLOSE and eject.



balenaEtcher (any OS)

Flash from file → the ISO.
Select target → the stick. Etcher hides system disks by default, which is the main reason to prefer it if dd makes you nervous.
Flash!, enter your password, wait for validation to finish.



Raspberry Pi Imager (SD cards, ARM images)

CHOOSE DEVICE → your board, or No filtering for the generic .img.xz.
CHOOSE OS → Other general-purpose OS → Ubuntu → Ubuntu Server 26.04 LTS (64-bit), or Use custom for a downloaded file.
CHOOSE STORAGE → the card.
In OS customisation, set hostname, username, password, and paste your SSH public key, then enable SSH. This writes cloud-init user-data to the boot partition so the board comes up headless — no monitor needed at all.
WRITE.



dd (macOS)

# 1. Identify the stick — note the disk number, e.g. disk4
diskutil list

# 2. Unmount it (but do not eject it)
diskutil unmountDisk /dev/disk4

# 3. Write the image to the RAW device (/dev/rdiskN is much faster than /dev/diskN)
sudo dd if=ubuntu-26.04-live-server-amd64.iso of=/dev/rdisk4 bs=4m

# 4. Eject
diskutil eject /dev/disk4







Note



macOS dd prints nothing while working. Press Ctrl+T to print progress. A 2.7 GiB write takes roughly 2–5 minutes on USB 3.




dd (Linux)

# 1. Identify the stick by size and model
lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,MODEL,MOUNTPOINTS

# 2. Write, then flush kernel buffers before unplugging
sudo dd if=ubuntu-26.04-live-server-amd64.iso of=/dev/sdX bs=4M status=progress oflag=sync
sync

Replace sdX with the whole device (sdb), never a partition (sdb1).

title: Setup
text:
Prepare BIOS/UEFI on the Server
Reboot the target machine and hold the setup key during power-on — F2, F10, F12, Del, or Esc depending on vendor. Then:

Boot order: put the USB stick first, or use the one-time boot menu.
Secure Boot: leave it on. Ubuntu’s bootloader and kernel are signed by Canonical, so it boots fine. Only third-party out-of-tree drivers require turning it off.
Fast Boot / Ultra Fast Boot: turn off, otherwise USB devices are not enumerated early enough to boot from.
Restore on AC Power Loss: set to Power On (sometimes Last State). Without this, the server stays dark after a power cut until you walk over and press the button.
Virtualisation (VT-x, AMD-V, SVM, plus VT-d/IOMMU): enable if you plan on VMs.
Wake-on-LAN: enable if you want to power the box up remotely later.

Save, exit, and boot the stick. After a few seconds you land on the installer’s language screen.

title: Setup
text:
Run the Installer
The installer is subiquity, a text UI driven with arrow keys, Tab, Space, and Enter. Screens in order:

Language — English keeps log messages searchable.
Installer update — accept if offered; it pulls bug fixes for the installer itself.
Keyboard layout — set it correctly now or the password you type at first login will not be the one you set.
Type of install — Ubuntu Server (full). The minimized variant strips tooling meant for interactive administration, which is the opposite of what a homelab wants.
Network — the installer tries DHCP on wired interfaces. Let it, and pin a static address after first boot (below); doing it here works too but is fiddlier in a text UI. Note the assigned IP shown on this screen.
Proxy — leave empty unless your network requires one.
Mirror — geolocated automatically. Leave as-is; a wrong mirror only slows downloads.
Storage — Use an entire disk. Two decisions:

Set up this disk as an LVM group: yes. LVM lets you grow, shrink, and snapshot volumes later without reinstalling.
Encrypt the LVM group with LUKS: only if the machine could be stolen. An encrypted server cannot boot unattended — it waits at a passphrase prompt after every power cut, which defeats a headless box.

Confirm destructive action — the last exit before the disk is wiped. Re-read the device name.
Profile — your name, a server hostname (used everywhere afterwards: nas, lab01), username, password. This user is an administrator with sudo.
Ubuntu Pro — skip here, attach later in one command.
SSH — check Install OpenSSH server. Then set Import SSH identity to from GitHub and enter your GitHub username to pull your public keys. Importing a key disables password authentication automatically.
Featured snaps — select nothing. Install what you need later, from the repo you actually want it from.
Install log — wait for Reboot Now, then pull the USB stick when prompted.







Note



No SSH keys on GitHub yet? Generate a pair on your laptop first — see Git & GitHub Setup — and push the public key there before you reach this screen. Otherwise you fall back to password login and have to run ssh-copy-id afterwards.

title: Setup
text:
First Login
On the server console, log in and find its address:

ip -brief address
hostnamectl

From your laptop:

ssh <username>@<ip-address>

If you skipped the key import, copy your key over now and never type that password again:

ssh-copy-id <username>@<ip-address>

Unplug the monitor and keyboard. Everything below is over SSH.

title: Setup
text:
Baseline Hardening and Housekeeping
Run these once, in order. Each is small and independently useful.

Patch Everything

sudo apt update && sudo apt full-upgrade -y
sudo reboot        # only if /var/run/reboot-required exists

Check whether a reboot is actually needed:

ls /var/run/reboot-required 2>/dev/null && cat /var/run/reboot-required.pkgs



Hostname and Timezone

sudo hostnamectl set-hostname lab01
sudo timedatectl set-timezone Asia/Seoul
timedatectl status

26.04 uses chrony as the time daemon (it replaced systemd-timesyncd for new installs) with authenticated NTP against Canonical’s servers. Confirm sync:

chronyc tracking



Static IP with Netplan
A server whose address moves is a server you cannot find. Either reserve a DHCP lease on your router (simplest, keeps config in one place) or pin it on the host. For the latter, find the interface name and write a new Netplan file — do not edit the cloud-init one:

ip -brief link


sudo tee /etc/netplan/99-homelab.yaml > /dev/null <<'EOF'
network:
  version: 2
  renderer: networkd
  ethernets:
    enp1s0:
      dhcp4: false
      addresses:
        - 192.168.0.50/24
      routes:
        - to: default
          via: 192.168.0.1
      nameservers:
        addresses: [192.168.0.1, 1.1.1.1]
EOF
sudo chmod 600 /etc/netplan/99-homelab.yaml

Apply with the safety net — netplan try reverts automatically after 120 seconds if you do not confirm, so a typo cannot lock you out:

sudo netplan try







Note



Netplan warns about world-readable config because these files can hold Wi-Fi secrets. The chmod 600 above is what silences it.




Lock Down SSH
Never edit /etc/ssh/sshd_config directly; drop a file into the include directory so package upgrades stay conflict-free.

sudo tee /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-homelab.conf > /dev/null <<'EOF'
PermitRootLogin no
PasswordAuthentication no
KbdInteractiveAuthentication no
EOF
sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl reload ssh

sshd -t validates the config first — reloading a broken config is how people lose access to headless machines.






Warning



Confirm key-based login works in a second terminal before closing your current session. With PasswordAuthentication no and no working key, your only way back in is a physical keyboard.


26.04 ships OpenSSH 10.2, which drops DSA keys entirely and negotiates post-quantum key exchange (mlkem768x25519-sha256) by default. PerSourcePenalties is also on by default, temporarily blocking addresses that keep failing authentication — useful, and one reason fail2ban is now optional rather than essential.


Firewall

sudo ufw allow OpenSSH
sudo ufw enable
sudo ufw status verbose

Order matters: allow SSH before enabling, or you cut your own connection.


Automatic Security Updates

sudo apt install -y unattended-upgrades
sudo dpkg-reconfigure --priority=low unattended-upgrades

Optionally let it reboot itself in the small hours when a kernel update requires it:

sudo tee /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/52homelab-reboot > /dev/null <<'EOF'
Unattended-Upgrade::Automatic-Reboot "true";
Unattended-Upgrade::Automatic-Reboot-Time "04:30";
EOF

Dry-run to see what it would do:

sudo unattended-upgrade --dry-run --debug



Attach Ubuntu Pro (Free)
Free for personal use on up to 5 machines. It extends security coverage from 5 to 10 years, adds ESM for the much larger universe repository, and enables Livepatch (kernel patches without reboots — now on ARM64 too). Get a token from ubuntu.com/pro/dashboard:

sudo pro attach <your-token>
sudo pro status

title: Setup
text:
Laptop and Power Behaviour
If the server is a laptop, it will suspend when you close the lid and vanish from the network. Tell logind to ignore the lid:

sudo mkdir -p /etc/systemd/logind.conf.d
sudo tee /etc/systemd/logind.conf.d/99-homelab.conf > /dev/null <<'EOF'
[Login]
HandleLidSwitch=ignore
HandleLidSwitchDocked=ignore
HandleLidSwitchExternalPower=ignore
EOF
sudo systemctl restart systemd-logind

For any headless machine, mask sleep outright:

sudo systemctl mask sleep.target suspend.target hibernate.target hybrid-sleep.target

title: Setup
text:
26.04 LTS Specifics Worth Knowing
Coming from 24.04 or from older tutorials, these changes bite:

sudo is now sudo-rs, a Rust reimplementation. It reads the same /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d/, so ordinary use is identical. Exotic options may be unsupported; the original is still installed as sudo.ws.
Core utilities come from rust-coreutils (uutils). GNU versions remain available with a gnu prefix, e.g. gnuls, gnusort. Scripts relying on GNU-only flags may need it. To switch the whole system:

# GNU
sudo apt install coreutils-from-gnu --allow-remove-essential
# back to Rust
sudo apt install coreutils-from-uutils --allow-remove-essential

cp, mv, and rm are still GNU implementations regardless.
cgroup v1 is gone (systemd 259). Any container runtime or tooling still expecting the legacy hierarchy will not start. Current Docker and k3s are fine.
/tmp is a tmpfs, so it lives in RAM and is wiped on reboot. Do not stage a 40 GB restore there.
APT 3 removed apt-key. Third-party repos must place their key in /etc/apt/keyrings/ and reference it with signed-by=.
System V init script support is deprecated — this is the last LTS that honours it. Write systemd units.
amd64v3 packages are opt-in and build for the x86-64-v3 microarchitecture (roughly any AMD64 CPU from the last decade). Free performance if your hardware qualifies:

echo 'APT::Architecture-Variants "amd64v3";' | sudo tee /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/99enable-amd64v3
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade

The real-time kernel is free in 26.04, outside Ubuntu Pro. Irrelevant for most homelabs, handy for audio or industrial I/O.

title: Setup
text:
Where to Go Next
Container runtime, from Docker’s own repo (it resolves to the resolute suite for 26.04):

sudo install -m 0755 -d /etc/apt/keyrings
sudo curl -fsSL https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu/gpg -o /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc
sudo chmod a+r /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc
echo "deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture) signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc] \
https://download.docker.com/linux/ubuntu $(. /etc/os-release && echo "$VERSION_CODENAME") stable" \
  | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.list > /dev/null
sudo apt update
sudo apt install -y docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin
sudo usermod -aG docker $USER   # log out and back in to take effect

Or skip straight to the orchestrator this section uses:

curl -sfL https://get.k3s.io | sh -
sudo k3s kubectl get nodes







Note



Adding your user to the docker group is equivalent to giving it root — the daemon runs as root and the socket is the API. Fine on a homelab you own, not fine on a shared host.

title: Setup
text:
Repeatable Installs (Optional)
Building more than one node? Do not click through the installer repeatedly. Subiquity reads a cloud-init autoinstall file, so an identical node can be provisioned unattended: put user-data and an empty meta-data in the root of a second USB stick labelled CIDATA, boot the normal installer stick alongside it, and the install runs with no keyboard input.
The lazy way to author that file is to install one machine by hand, then copy the config it wrote:

sudo cat /var/log/installer/autoinstall-user-data

Edit the hostname, user, and SSH keys, and reuse it for the rest of the fleet.
